Clients generalize locally updated privacy rules and selectively incorporate globally maintained rules, thereby facilitating cross-client privacy rule evolution while preserving personalized constraints. Extensive experiments across reasoning, privacy sensitive, and adversarial settings show that PFedMA improves task performance, reduces measured privacy leakage, and improves system robustness.

title: MIPS: Mitigating Mode Collapse in Reinforcement Learning for Large Outcome Spaces
authors: Armaan Sandhu, Abhijeet Sinha, Dianbo Liu
abstract: Expected-reward maximization in reinforcement learning concentrates probability mass on a few outcomes, even in tasks that require many distinct, high-quality solutions, a failure known as mode collapse. Inverse Probability Scaling (IPS) counters this in group-based policy gradients such as GRPO by dividing each reward by the outcome's probability, estimated from its frequency within the sampled group. When the outcome space is large relative to the group, outcomes rarely repeat and these estimates become uninformative. Since an outcome can be constructed along many trajectories, its probability is a sum over all of them, and computing it directly is intractable. We propose Marginal IPS (MIPS), which performs marginal evaluation by combining the sampled trajectory with a learned model of the trajectories that lead to each outcome. On Hypergrids, where the exact sampling distribution is computable, MIPS stays near the reward-distribution target as the outcome space grows relative to the rollout group, while frequency-based IPS degrades. In molecular synthesis and phylogenetic inference, MIPS sustains diverse, high-quality sampling where GRPO and frequency-based IPS collapse, showing that MIPS serves as a reliable solution to mode collapse in RL.

title: Large-Step Last-Iterate Convergence of Random-Reshuffling Stochastic Gradient Descent
authors: Zijun Chen, Zihan Zhang
abstract: Random reshuffling stochastic gradient descent (RR-SGD) is widely used for finite-sum optimization in machine learning. For convex $L$-smooth components, recent work establishes convergence guarantees for an averaged iterate with component stepsizes as large as order $1/L$. However, the final iterate is a natural output in practice, and existing last-iterate guarantees in this setting require stepsizes that scale inversely with the number of components $n$. We establish an expected objective-gap bound for the last iterate of standard RR-SGD on unconstrained problems with a constant component stepsize satisfying $0<η\lesssim 1/(L(1 + \log(nK)))$, where $K$ is the number of epochs. By retaining the sampling bias at random comparison points, we remove the explicit $1/n$ factor from the stepsize restriction. Combined with existing small-step bounds, our result matches the corresponding averaged-iterate convergence rate up to logarithmic factors.

title: More Than Seeing: Vision as Scalable Anchors in Native Multimodal Pre-Training
authors: Haoyuan Wu, Aoqi Wu, Jiani Hu, Bei Yu
abstract: Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance.

title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Shuyuan Zheng, Yun-seo Lee, Xing Gao, Jialu Wu, Jiabao Hu, Katrina Qiyao Wang, Xinbo Lin, Qianying Liu, Chuan Xiao, Tao Huang
abstract: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. Existing research has largely overlooked whether LLMs can understand legal philosophy and apply it in legal reasoning, an ability we call \textit{legal-philosophical reasoning}. To fill this gap, we introduce LePhilBench, a benchmark for evaluating the legal-philosophical reasoning of LLMs that comprises two benchmarking tasks and a dataset. The two tasks evaluate how well LLMs understand legal philosophy and how well they apply it in legal reasoning, respectively. The dataset is manually and meticulously constructed. Its test set contains 220 U.S. Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions on legal philosophy, and three law-trained annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all fourteen questions for every opinion, yielding 9,240 legal-philosophical labels. LePhilBench takes the first step toward exploring legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs.

title: Beyond the Trial-and-Error Loop: Hybrid Projection and Automated Tuning for Distributed Training
authors: Anshu Raina, Peyman Razaghi, Yuankai Chen, Cheng Yao, Yao Fu, Vidushi Goyal, Devang Patel, Wen Xie, Zhenyu Gu, Emad Barsoum
abstract: Configuring distributed LLM training across hundreds of GPUs requires jointly optimizing tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism alongside micro-batch size, recomputation, sharding, and overlap, a combinatorial space where memory legality can hinge on a single byte of activation accounting. Today, teams navigate it through expensive multi-node trial and error, burning GPU-hours on crashes and suboptimal recipes. We present Primus Projection, which closes this loop with two coupled components. First, a hybrid projection engine that measures what it can and simulates what it cannot: GPU microbenchmarks on as few as a single device capture compute kernels and any in-scope communication; a sub-node downscale-measure-upscale workflow analytically restores out-of-scope collectives, FSDP overlap, and the full pipeline schedule at the multi-node target. A pure simulation mode runs entirely on CPU, enabling pre-silicon planning without any GPU. Second, the Primus Tuning Agent treats the projection engine as a fast scoring oracle (seconds per candidate instead of tens of minutes) and uses it to drive an intelligent search over the configuration space. A deterministic seed planner sweeps single axes; an LLM investigation loop proposes cross-axis combinations the planner cannot reach, with an analytic memory pre-filter that rejects infeasible candidates before any GPU time is spent. Validated on Llama 3.1 (dense) and Mixtral 8x22B (MoE) across two GPU generations, all projections stay within ~10% of measured multi-node throughput, and fidelity holds at production scale: 4.7% error on DeepSeek V3 671B at 1,024 GPUs and 1.9% on Qwen3-235B-A22B at 256 GPUs. In a Mixtral 8x22B case study, the Primus Tuning Agent discovers a configuration delivering +27% throughput over the published 4-node BF16 reference at the same scale, in under 30 minutes of single-node exploration.

title: Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities
authors: Hang Lin
abstract: We introduce FormCraft, a framework for representing acquired operations as first-class capabilities that can be recursively composed, directly invoked, and selectively retained in a persistent library through domain-specific verification. The framework separates capability well-formedness and public callability from later admission to persistent storage while preserving formation provenance and operational identity. We formalize recursive compositional closure over a uniform capability space and show that formed composites can be reused through the same public interface without re-forming their historical derivation. Experiments across continuous, discrete, propositional, and sequence domains demonstrate instance-independent reuse, independent checking, persistent acquisition, and reduced reuse-time search work under first-class exposure.

title: W-JEPA: Wavelet Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Wearable Activity Recognition
authors: Yogesh Prabhu, Loki Natarajan, Jingjing Zou
abstract: A major challenge in wearable device activity recognition is the heterogeneity across datasets in sensor placement, channel count, sampling rate and subjects. Moreover, the motion patterns that distinguish activities often appear as subtle, scale-specific variations within otherwise similar waveforms. As a result, raw signals are often ambiguous, and models trained on them tend to rely on cues specific to a particular sensor setup or participant, which limits both cross-dataset transfer and generalization to unseen participants. Addressing this requires representations that preserve such activity-relevant, scale-specific variation. We introduce W-JEPA, a self-supervised framework that exploits the multiscale structure of inertial motion and leverages a joint-embedding predictive architecture, by organizing windows into a fixed grid of wavelet tokens indexed by scale, sensor axis, and time. These wavelet tokens help expose activity-specific detail within broadly similar raw signals, and serve as the units of masked latent prediction. W-JEPA predicts masked token representations supplied by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder. Because recovering a masked token requires relating motion at one scale and axis to motion at other scales and axes, the model learns the cross-scale, cross-axis structure of human movement. Across six wearable activity benchmarks, W-JEPA outperforms state-of-the-art methods under random-window splits and remains the strongest when subjects are held out, improving average macro-F1 by 8.7 percentage points over the strongest published baseline. These results indicate that physically grounded multiscale tokenization, combined together with latent predictive learning, provides a promising foundation for transferable representations of heterogeneous wearable inertial data.

title: Fractional elementary symmetric functions and Hessian estimates in the plane
authors: Gautam Neelakantan Memana, Neil S. Trudinger, Po-Lam Yung
abstract: We prove an endpoint Pucci maximum principle for domains in $\mathbb R^2$, formulated using a generalization of elementary symmetric polynomials to noninteger orders. As a result, we sharpen an earlier result of Astala, Iwaniec and Martin, and deduce a new Sobolev inequality for $q$-Hessians where $1 < q < 2$. The fractional elementary symmetric functions we use are derived through fractional differentiation. Their signed singular value extension coincides with the Burkholder functional introduced by Burkholder and gives us access to a local Burkholder inequality due to Astala, Iwaniec, Prause and Saksman, leading to a different proof of the Pucci maximum principle from the one in that used quasiconformal maps. We include an elementary real-variable proof of this local Burkholder inequality, obtained by combining a few known techniques from existing literature.

title: Weight-adapted ANOVA kernels for high-dimensional periodic approximation
authors: Zhengjie Sun
abstract: In this paper, we construct normalized periodic kernels from univariate functions satisfying suitable moment conditions and derive sufficient conditions for high-order convolution approximation. Two computable quasi-interpolation schemes are obtained by discretizing the convolution integral using either a full tensor grid or random samples. In each case, the analysis separates the continuous convolution error from the error introduced by discretization. The contribution of kernel energy to the error exposes the dimensional dependence of tensor-product kernels and motivates our weight-adapted ANOVA constructions. Under suitable summability conditions on the weights, we establish convolution error and kernel energy estimates that yield dimension-uniform error bounds for the resulting quasi-interpolants. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical convergence rates and illustrate the effect of coordinate weighting on dimensional dependence.

title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
authors: Javad Mirzaei, Jeebak Mitra
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.

title: RA$^2$: Retain-Anchored Attraction Preserves Forget-Adjacent Utility in LLM Unlearning
authors: Zinan Ling, Yang Xiao, Ruimeng Ye, Sijia Liu, Bo Hui
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning is often evaluated primarily by target suppression and clean retain utility. These metrics can miss a local failure mode: a model may perform well on standard retain prompts, yet degrade on benign reasoning when prompts lie near the forgotten domain. This phenomenon is termed forget-adjacent utility loss. A fundamental question is: where should forget representations go after they leave the removed behavior? Successful unlearning depends not only on whether forget-conditioned representations depart from the harmful computation, but also on the direction in which they are redirected afterward. We propose RA$^2$ (Retain-Anchored Attraction), a latent-space unlearning method that redirects forget-token states toward nearby retain-supported representations while preserving higher-layer behavior on retain data. On WMDP and MUSE, RA$^2$ yields higher forget-adjacent utility than strong unlearning baselines at similar broad-utility levels. These results show that the migration direction of forget representations materially affects benign behavior near the forget boundary. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZacLing/retain_anchored_attraction.

title: EvoWeave: Composing Reusable Agent Experience through Operation Level Graphs
authors: Guanhua Zhu, Bo Shen, Lei Zhang, Fadi Deek, Zhi Wei, Mengnan Du, Chenxi Yuan
abstract: Different tasks often require interactive agents to perform similar operations at intermediate steps. Retrieving an entire past workflow can introduce irrelevant steps, whereas retrieving isolated operations can discard the dependencies needed to reuse them. We introduce EvoWeave, a framework for experience memory that represents abstract states as nodes and reusable operations as directed edges with input and output contracts, provenance, and capability references. A planner decomposes the current task into a dependency graph; operation retrieval and bounded directed search then assemble relevant experience fragments. An execution agent can inspect these fragments and their referenced capabilities, while reflection separates concrete execution evidence from reusable abstractions. We study the framework across four benchmarks, five evaluation settings, and three language model backbones. Across backbones, AppWorld Normal and Challenge task goal completion average 51.91 and 27.99, respectively, exceeding the baseline without memory by 6.99 and 4.99 percentage points. An AppWorld ablation associates directed connections with an additional improvement of 2.08 points over independent operation cards. The results motivate composition of reusable operations while exposing tradeoffs in retrieval overhead and conditions for valid reuse.

title: Policy-Verified Self-Training: Learning Agent Compliance from Verifiable Policy Rewards
authors: Min-Young Yu
abstract: Runtime policy verifiers can prevent agents from executing disallowed actions, but their decisions are typically used only for enforcement and discarded afterward. We ask whether these decisions can instead become verifiable policy rewards for training the agents they guard. We introduce Policy-Verified Self-Training (PVST), a post-training paradigm in which an agent generates its own interaction trajectories and an executable policy verifier, here a deterministic gate compiled from a written policy, evaluates whether each action complies. Compliant trajectories are reinforced, and violations become negatives for preference optimization; beyond the gate and the benchmark's task-success signal, PVST needs no stronger teacher model, no human preference labels and no attack-specific supervision, although rollouts are collected in the benchmark's attacked environment. On held-out AgentDojo tasks under prompt injection, policy-verified preference training of Qwen3-8B reduces violating trajectories from 37.2% to 10.3 $\pm$ 0.9% (three seeds) and successful attacks from 12.4% to 0.5% at equal or higher pooled task utility, although utility falls on travel, compared with 22.0% when negatives are selected by an attack oracle and 31.9 $\pm$ 0.9% with negatives that contain no violation. The learned behavior holds under an attack template never used in training (37.7% to 11.0%) and on a suite excluded from training (34.8% to 16.7%), and the retained verifier's intervention rate falls from 39.2% to 8.8% (seed 0). Our analysis identifies two conditions under which the verdict is most informative: success must not already imply compliance, and guarded actions must appear in both permitted and forbidden contexts.

title: Where to Start, How to Move: Analyzing Curricula under GRPO for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
authors: Minchan Kim, Sungho Bae, Youngjin Kim, Hyunwoo Park
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) provides no reward-relative learning signal when all rollouts receive identical rewards. In long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions, rewards are given only upon successful task completion, making all-fail groups common early in training and limiting opportunities to practice later steps. Guide Assisted GRPO replays a successful reference prefix before the learner continues. We study how initial positions, handoff units, and movement rules affect unassisted task completion. Across three model sizes on BFCL, starting near completion is more effective under a fixed turn-level threshold rule. Finer handoffs alone do not consistently help, but outcome-informed tool-call selection outperforms GRPO on trained and untrained task categories. Guided starts also improve AppWorld success on both evaluation splits. These findings highlight where learning starts and how starting positions move as key curriculum choices.

title: Integrated Novelty Detection Systems: From Sensor Networks to Multi-Novelty Computer Vision
authors: Irené Tematelewo
abstract: Novelty detection is crucial in various technological and scientific domains. Its importance spans from ensuring the reliability of sensor networks to enhancing the adaptability of computer vision systems. As AI systems become increasingly sophisticated and complex, effective anomaly detection is essential for maintaining reliability and accuracy. This work addresses novelty detection in weather sensor networks and computer vision. In weather sensor networks, particularly for monitoring rainfall, detecting blocked rain gauges can significantly impact data reliability, food security, and disaster management. This work evaluates four existing quality control methods for detecting blocked rain gauges and demonstrates their limitations, particularly in detecting clusters of faulty sensors. By comparing methods such as the Conditional Mixture Model (CMM), PSWQ (Fz-filter), Kernel Regression, and Gaussian Method, we identify their shortcomings and propose three novel quality control techniques that integrate probabilistic fault detection and consistency-based diagnosis framework to improve timely detection of blocked sensors, while reducing false alarms. In the realm of computer vision, current systems often fail to handle multiple types of novelty due to their focus on single-novelty scenarios. We highlight the need for integrated systems capable of handling multiple types of novelty. To support this, we introduce the Novel Snapshot Serengeti (NOVEL-SS) dataset, derived from the Snapshot Serengeti camera trap data, which includes various forms of novelty. We also present the DCA (Detect, Characterize, and Accommodate) baseline system, designed to handle multiple novelty by detecting, characterizing, and accommodating them. This work aims to advance the robustness and adaptability of novelty detection systems across both weather sensor networks and computer vision applications.

title: Can We Believe AI Peer Review?
authors: Zongrui Yang, Haoyuan Li, Zhongsheng Wang, Gillian Dobbie, Jiamou Liu
abstract: As large language models become widely used in scientific review and manuscript revision, AI scores are increasingly serving as feedback for assessing paper quality and guiding edits. Yet whether a single AI score reliably reflects the reviewer's judgment, and whether revision gains based on that score are endorsed by other reviewers, remain understudied. Using 200 papers from ICLR 2025 and 2026 and approximately 14,000 AI reviews, we study score reliability, score-distribution estimation, and cross-model agreement on revision gains. Repeated reviews fluctuate even under identical conditions. Finer-grained scoring protocols reduce score variance but also systematically shift mean scores, while the gains assigned to manuscript revisions depend strongly on the reviewer.

title: Nondegeneracy and asymptotic behavior of type I blow-up for semilinear heat equations with general nonlinearities
authors: Yohei Fujishima, Ryoto Ichiya, Norisuke Ioku
abstract: We study the local asymptotic behavior of nonnegative type I blow-up solutions to semilinear heat equations with nonlinearities that need not be scale invariant. Using a quasi-similarity transformation adapted to the associated ordinary differential equation, we establish locally uniform convergence to a constant profile on the parabolic spatial scale near every interior blow-up point. Under a quantitative assumption on the nonlinearity at infinity, our results cover regularly varying nonlinearities in the Sobolev subcritical and critical ranges and, in one and two space dimensions, rapidly growing nonlinearities including double exponentials. A key ingredient in this analysis is a positive lower bound for the normalized solution at interior blow-up points. In fact, under weaker assumptions on the nonlinearity, we prove this bound in arbitrary space dimension without assuming radial symmetry.

title: Search for Sub-Solar Mass Binaries in the First and Second Part of LIGO's Fourth Observing Run O4a-O4b
authors: Keisi Kacanja, Kanchan Soni, Alexander H. Nitz
abstract: The observation of sub-solar mass neutron stars and black holes would signify a new class of astrophysical objects since these systems are not expected to form via standard stellar evolution. We present the first sub-solar mass search for binaries consisting of neutron star or black holes that uses the data from both the second part (O4b) and first part (O4a) of the fourth observing run of the Advanced LIGO detectors. The search covers primary masses 0.1 to 2 $M_\odot$ and secondary masses 0.1 to 1 $M_\odot$. Tidal effects up to $7\times10^5$ are accounted for in extremely low-mass neutron stars. No statistically significant candidates are identified. We place a $90\%$ confidence upper limit on the merger rate $\mathcal{R}_{90}$ for sub-solar mass black holes and neutron stars to be $< 5.2\times10^{2}\,\textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\,\textrm{yr}^{-1}$ for a chirp mass of 0.5 $M_\odot$, a factor $2.2 \times$ lower compared to previous O1-O4a searches. We constrain the effective local dark matter fraction to be $\tilde{f}_\textrm{PBH}<0.6\%$ for $M_{\textrm{PBH}}=0.8 \,M_\odot$, approximately $1.5$ factor improvement to previous O1-O4a constraints. Given our model assumptions, our local dark matter fraction constraints are $2-7$ times lower than the OGLE microlensing survey for $M_{\textrm{PBH}}\ge{0.6}~M_\odot$.

title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
authors: Zefan Yang, Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Maihe, Yikang Liu, Hang Yu, Ankush Mukherjee, Xiao Chen, Pingkun Yan, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.

title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action
authors: Ao Liang, Youquan Liu, Mingxiao Li, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Yue Liao, Dongyue Lu, Yu Yang, Wei Yin, Runnan Chen
abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard. Project page: https://worldbench.github.io/vital

title: DynThinker: Unifying Static 3D and Dynamic 4D Spatial Reasoning
authors: Qihang Cao, Haoyuan Li, Zihan Guo, Sensen Gao, Zihui Gao, Huixin Zhang, Fan He, Jianhua Han, Hang Xu, Xiaodan Liang, Jia-Wang Bian
abstract: Achieving general spatial intelligence requires a unified understanding of both static 3D and dynamic 4D. However, we find that existing models struggle to excel at both: 3D post-training can weaken dynamic understanding, while 4D-specialized models often lack strong static 3D reasoning. Our analysis reveals that this spatial--dynamic interference is highly non-uniform across parameter groups, with the balance between static and dynamic capabilities particularly sensitive to changes in late-layer MLPs. To address this interference, we propose DynThinker, a unified framework for jointly strengthening static and dynamic spatial reasoning. Decoupled Exponential Moving Average (D-EMA) applies configurable group-wise averaging to constrain drift in interference-sensitive pretrained parameters while preserving flexibility for capability enhancement. Spatial-Dynamic Fusion (SDF) complements D-EMA by selectively integrating spatial and temporal priors from a dynamic geometry encoder into intermediate VLM representations under semantic guidance. Across ten metrics spanning nine static 3D and dynamic 4D benchmarks, DynThinker achieves the highest average score among all evaluated models. Notably, DynThinker achieves 56.0 on ReVSI, 67.2 on DSR-Bench, and 51.2 and 40.1 under the sample-wise and group-wise evaluation protocols of DSI-Bench, respectively, setting new state-of-the-art results among the compared open-source models across all four evaluations within a unified model.

title: The $\mathrm{U}$-Derivative Associated with Linear Recurrence Sequences
authors: Ronald Orozco López
abstract: We associate a canonical operator to every linear recurrence sequence admitting a distinct-root Binet representation \(\mathrm{U}_n=\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_jλ_j^n.\) The construction is based on the spectral Binet operator \(\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{U}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_jT_{λ_j}, \) where \(T_{λ_j}f(x)=f(λ_jx)\) is the dilation operator associated with the characteristic root \(λ_j\). The corresponding recurrence derivative is defined by \(\mathrm{D}_\mathrm{U}=x^{-1}\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{U}.\) Its fundamental property is the monomial identity \(\mathrm{D}_\mathrm{U}(x^n)=\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1},\) which establishes a direct correspondence between recurrence sequences and degree-lowering operators. We develop the operator theory of \(\mathrm{D}_\mathrm{U}\), including iteration, a spectral product rule, the associated Leibniz defect, and a quotient rule. The construction reveals a natural bifurcation determined by the value \(\mathrm{U}_0\), producing the Ward and non-Ward regimes as intrinsic operatorial phenomena. The product structure is shown to be governed by \(k-2\) residual spectral channels, leading to notions of spectral cancellation and spectral balance. As an application, we obtain a complete qualitative classification of second-order recurrence calculi. Using Horadam sequences as a universal second-order model, we prove that every such calculus is determined by the invariant triple \((\mathrm{W}_0,Δ, Z_\mathrm{W}),\) where \(\mathrm{W}_0\) identifies the Ward/non-Ward type, \(Δ\) determines the spectral geometry, and \(Z_\mathrm{W}\) determines regularity or singularity.

title: GeoThinker-$F$: Endogenous Predictive World Representations for Fast Spatial Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Qihang Cao, Huanyuan Zhou, Xin Hu, Sijia Chen, Zihan Guo, Kun Xiang, Yunshuang Nie, Tao Tang, Xinlong Zheng, Jia-Wang Bian, Xianming Liu, Xiaodan Liang
abstract: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful representations of current geometry and future semantics, without requiring an exact reproduction of features from a dedicated 3D encoder. To realize this idea, GeoThinker-$F$ adopts a decoupled two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, the MLLM backbone is frozen while lightweight Latent Frame Prediction (LFP) heads learn from an offline 3D geometry expert and next-frame semantic targets. In the second stage, the external expert is removed, and the model is jointly optimized to generate and selectively integrate its self-predicted priors through a specialized Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion module. Extensive evaluations show that GeoThinker-$F$ eliminates runtime dependence on external 3D geometry encoders while maintaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks. It achieves up to a $3.6\times$ inference speedup, reducing latency from $1.45\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.40\,\mathrm{s}$ while retaining strong spatial reasoning performance.

title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
authors: Walter Simoncini, Dheeraj Varghese, Gertjan J. Burghouts, Cees G. M. Snoek
abstract: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders ranging from 22M to 8B parameters, our method yields smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity and outperforms one-shot baselines under deep pruning. For example, pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters while reducing ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy by only 0.8%, without the need for weight correction or retraining. At 60% sparsity, a pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 model achieves up to $1.80\times$ higher throughput and $1.26\times$ lower single-query latency on an A100 GPU. Elastic models are produced in minutes, with construction time scaling sub-linearly with parameter count.

title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
authors: Shubhendu Trivedi, Jacob Eisenstein, Alekh Agarwal, Ian Gemp, Michael Kaisers, Adam Fisch
abstract: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.

title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training
authors: Yingfa Chen, Xingyu Shen, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han
abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction

title: GRB 181201A: Spectropolarimetric Constraints on Prompt Emission and Magnetic Field Structure
authors: Dhruv S. Bal, Nikita S. Khatiya, Philippe Laurent, Diego Götz, Dieter H. Hartmann, Ramandeep Gill
abstract: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) have served as testbeds for high-energy astrophysical phenomena since their discovery over 50 years ago. GRB detections reveal diverse properties across events, complicating efforts to constrain their emission mechanisms, magnetic fields, jet structures, and compositions. Spectropolarimetry is a powerful tool utilized to disentangle these properties. INTEGRAL/IBIS has previously detected three polarized GRBs 041219A ($65\pm 26$%), 061122 ($>$33%) and 140206A ($>$28%). We present the time-integrated and time-resolved analyses of the fourth-polarized GRB 181201A. This GRB exhibits high polarization ($81.5^{+17.2}_{-15.7}$%) over three time bins with the highest signal-to-noise ratio, and the polarization angle (PA) shows a modest temporal evolution. The photon index does not cross the synchrotron line-of-death and shows a hard-to-soft evolution. A high degree of polarization (PD) tends to disfavor a photospheric emission model, as previous studies indicate that this model yields PD $<$ 20%. A modest evolution in the PA points towards a non-axisymmetric jet with a multi-patch emission. Our results indicate that under standard synchrotron conditions, the magnetic field is coherent but lacks global structure. Moreover, the field has multiple patches, but only one or a few dominate due to high degrees of polarization, which overlap with the intrinsic maximum of synchrotron emission within 3$σ$ errors. The high PD is also indicative of the Compton Drag scenario, but only under certain conditions, such as viewing the relativistic jet near its edge. However, given our error bars and the scope for improvement in our pipeline, we cannot strongly favor either scenario; both may remain viable.

title: Every Gromov elliptic domain is meromorphically pseudoconvex
authors: Yuta Kusakabe
abstract: We prove that every Gromov elliptic domain $Ω$ in a complex manifold has the following property, which we call meromorphic pseudoconvexity: each boundary point has a neighborhood $V$ such that $Ω\cap V$ becomes Stein after removing a set which is, locally in $Ω\cap V$, the union of the polar sets of finitely many meromorphic functions on $Ω\cap V$. Since meromorphic functions on Hartogs figures extend to their hulls, it follows that, for a domain $Ω=\operatorname{int}\overlineΩ$ in a Stein manifold, Gromov ellipticity is equivalent to being Oka and Stein, and also to being Oka and admitting a complete Kähler metric. This complements a theorem of Matsumura and the author that every weakly pseudoconvex Oka manifold admitting a positive line bundle is elliptic. As applications, we show that the Oka manifolds $\mathbb C^n\setminus\overline{\mathbb B^n}$ and $\mathbb C^n\setminus\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, are not elliptic, and that no proper domain with Lipschitz boundary in $\mathbb P^n$, $n\geq2$, is elliptic.

title: Complex generalized spin-c Killing spinors in low dimensions
authors: José Luis Carmona Jiménez, Alejandro Gil-García, C. S. Shahbazi
abstract: We classify all complex generalized spin-c Killing spinors with complex Killing function $iμ-α$ on complete Riemannian surfaces, presenting an explicit list of all possible cases. We show that, contrary to previous statements in the literature, there exist complex generalized spin-c Killing spinors on Riemannian surfaces for which $αμ\not\equiv0$. We illustrate the classification by providing several explicit local, compact, and complete examples, including a complete example for which $αμ>0$ everywhere. We then move to three dimensions, proving that a spin-c Riemannian three-manifold admits a complex generalized spin-c Killing spinor with complex Killing function $iμ-α$ if and only if it is a $μ$-exact trans-Sasakian manifold of type $(α,μ)$. In addition, we construct a geodesically incomplete Riemannian three-manifold equipped with a complex generalized spin-c Killing spinor for which neither $μ$ nor $α$ vanishes identically, and then prove that this is not possible if the characteristic vector field of the associated trans-Sasakian structure is complete. These results settle a conjecture by Große and Nakad (Results in Mathematics, 2015) stating that on two- and three-dimensional Riemannian manifolds the complex Killing function of any complex generalized spin-c Killing spinor must be either globally real or globally imaginary.

title: The large sieve inequality and additive decompositions of sums of squares
authors: Christian Elsholtz, Julia Stadlmann
abstract: Building on the large sieve, we prove a new sieve estimate for sets which are missing various residue classes modulo prime squares. For certain interesting residue class configurations, our bound is a significant improvement over the corresponding Johnsen-Selberg sieve inequality. Our application of this sieve estimate is motivated by Ostmann's problem. We study additive decompositions of sums of squares and show that any non-trivial sumset decomposition must consist of two sets of roughly equal size: If $A_1, A_2 \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $A_1 + A_2 = \{x^2 + y^2 : x, y \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ and $|A_1|, |A_2| \geq 2$, then $\sqrt{x}/(\log x)^{9/2} \ll |A_i \cap [1, x]| \ll \sqrt{x}(\log x)^4$ for $i \in \{1, 2\}$.

title: Reliability-Aware Multimodal Sentiment Prediction Under Local Modality Missingness
authors: Minghao Kong, Deng Yao, Xi Zhang, Ying Gao, Jiurun Chen, Zirong Liu, Rongjie Wang
abstract: Multimodal sentiment models are usually evaluated on complete utterances, yet streams often lose a contiguous span of text, audio, or video. We study local missingness on aligned CMU-MOSEI features. Our reliability-aware network (RM-Net) keeps the original temporal positions, represents unobserved positions with a learned token, outputs bounded per-modality intensity contributions gated by observation quality, and is trained with dual-view masking of contiguous segments. We fuse five RM-Net seeds with a LoRA-adapted BERT text expert, using a fusion weight that depends only on the visible fraction of content tokens. Architecture, checkpoint, and fusion choices were made on the validation split. On the held-out split, the fused model reaches a macro-F1 of 0.655 on clean inputs and 0.634 under 40\% mixed missingness; its two-view average exceeds the auxiliary-head baseline by 0.024 (95\% video-cluster bootstrap interval [0.003, 0.045]). Because this split was inspected during development, these numbers are not a blind test. For explanations, exact Shapley attributions over the eight modality subsets and position-level occlusion show that top-ranked positions reduce the predicted-class probability faster than random positions (AUC gap 0.113 on validation). We also describe an auditable word-level alignment pipeline for raw clips; its outputs do not feed the predictive models.

title: Revealing the Spatial Distribution of Dust and Plasma Solitary Waves in Jupiter's Innermost Magnetosphere Using Juno Waves Observations
authors: Wenyu Zhang, Hao Cao, William S. Kurth, Mitchell M. Shen, Darrelle Wilkinson, Donglai Ma, Martin Brennan, George Hospodarsky, Scott J. Bolton
abstract: Jupiter's faint ring system contains micron- and submicron-sized dust whose dynamics are influenced by the planet's rapidly rotating magnetic field. Optical observations have established the morphology of the main ring and halo, but tenuous dust close to Jupiter remains difficult to characterize. We analyze nearly a decade of in-situ Juno Waves electric-field measurements using a two-stage convolutional neural network to identify and classify dust impacts, solitary waves, and other plasma waves. These in-situ dust-impact detections reveal a radially evolving structure extending well inside the traditionally observed halo. In the innermost region, dust is concentrated in a compact, equatorially symmetric layer, indicating that the optical inner boundary does not mark the end of the dust population. Farther outward, the layer expands vertically into a broad halo before contracting toward the main ring, directly revealing the toroidal morphology of the Jovian halo. Dust number density is enhanced within the halo and near the main-ring--halo transition. The vertical distribution also develops hemispheric asymmetries that vary with radial distance, consistent with an influence of Jupiter's magnetic geometry on charged-dust dynamics. In contrast, solitary waves occur predominantly at high latitudes, and their mapped magnetic footprints show a strong spatial correspondence with Jovian auroral structures, particularly the main auroral oval. Together, these in-situ measurements extend the remote-sensing picture of Jupiter's rings and reveal previously unresolved dust and plasma structures in its innermost magnetosphere.

title: Physical Time as a Missing Dimension of Robot Policy Memory Dynamics
authors: Yushen Liang, Yue Peng, Baosheng Jin, Tianluo Zhang, Xinyu Zhang, Shuyi Zhou, Zhuoran Chen, Xinqi Liu, Shenji Wan
abstract: Existing robot policy memories typically evolve with observation sequences, implicitly treating each update as the same amount of physical time. Yet identical observation histories can span different durations and require different actions, exposing physical time as a missing dimension of policy memory. We introduce Temporal Flow Policy (TFP), which learns memory dynamics to retain past events and evolve the memory state over measured time intervals. Observations and prior memory determine the content and time scales of each transition; elapsed time determines how far the state advances. TFP conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies through this memory state and is trained with their native imitation objectives. We evaluate TFP with Diffusion Policy and $π_{0.5}$ through controlled comparisons of memory designs. These experiments show that successful timing depends on both measured intervals and retained history. TFP achieves higher average success than the recurrent and state-space memories we equip with the same intervals and than a variant that feeds the interval to a learned gate. Memory readouts recover the time since an event and motion information after occlusion. Changing the supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions, linking time inputs to behavior. Real-robot tasks requiring timing or memory, together with LIBERO evaluations, demonstrate benefits in physical and general manipulation. These results suggest viewing robot memory not as stored observation history, but as a state that retains past events and evolves with physical time.

title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation
authors: Fei Wu, Zhenrong Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jun Du
abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.

title: Measurement of electromagnetic transition form factors in two-photon collisions at BESIII
authors: Max Lellmann
abstract: The muon anomalous magnetic moment, $a_μ= (g-2)_μ/2$, shows a sizeable discrepancy between Standard Model (SM) predictions and direct measurements, hinting at either New Physics or limitations in modeling low-energy strong interactions. As the uncertainty in the SM predictions currently exceeds the experimental uncertainty by a substantial margin, further improvements in theoretical precision are essential to clarify the origin of this discrepancy. The SM theoretical uncertainty is dominated by hadronic processes. The hadronic light-by-light (HLbL) scattering contribution relies on highly accurate data for hadron production via two-photon fusion. Operating at $\sqrt{s}=3.773\,\text{GeV}$ with over $20\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, the BESIII experiment is ideally suited to probe these processes at small momentum transfers. By precisely measuring channels like $e^+e^-\to e^+ e^-π^0$ and $e^+e^-\to e^+ e^-π^0π^0$, BESIII provides the critical experimental input necessary to sharpen the SM prediction and clarify the true nature of the $a_μ$ anomaly.

title: Can bosenovae deplete the galactic dark matter?
authors: Samuel Gómez Gómez, Joshua Eby
abstract: No: neither through the bosenovae of gravitational atoms formed around stars and compact objects, nor through those of boson stars formed in the galactic dark-matter halo. We assume that all the dark matter consists of ultralight bosons with attractive self-interactions, which can be captured in the gravitational potential of astrophysical objects or condense into self-gravitating configurations. When these systems collapse in a bosenova, part of their mass is turned into relativistic radiation that escapes the galaxy. We bound the mass that a single object can eject and sum it over realistic models of the Milky Way and of other types of galaxies. For gravitational atoms, with realistic stellar populations and stellar evolution, the stars of the Milky Way deplete at most $ε^{\rm GA}_\star\simeq3\times10^{-9}$ of its halo, and the pump is equally negligible in other galaxies. The central black hole, Sgr A$^*$, could reach $ε^{\rm GA}\sim10^{-3}$, but only for a boson mass disfavoured by ultrafaint dwarf galaxies and beyond the validity of the perturbative treatment, where only a geometric bound on the dark matter flux is available. For boson stars feeding on the rest of the halo, these would radiate at most $\sim3\times10^{-5}$ of the Milky-Way halo and $0.1\%$ of a DF2-like one.

title: Modelling the 6.7 GHz Methanol Flaring in G358.93-0.03 Using the Maxwell-Bloch Framework
authors: Ningyan Fang, Toktam Rashidi, Yoshinori Yonekura, Vahid Anari, Ross A. Burns, Martin Houde, Fereshteh Rajabi
abstract: We model selected 6.7 GHz methanol flare profiles in G358.93-0.03 using the one-dimensional Maxwell-Bloch framework. The 2019 non-periodic flare, associated with an accretion burst, produced complex single-dish light curves characterized by sharp rises, multiple peaks, secondary structure, and extended decays. For six representative velocity channels, we model each light curve as a sum of scaled intensity responses from effective emitting systems driven by phenomenological pump pulses of fixed width but with component-dependent background rates, amplitudes, and arrival times. The inferred initial inverted column densities correspond to characteristic superradiance timescales $T_{R,0} \simeq 0.3$-$1.4~{\rm d}$, which are shorter than the adopted dephasing and relaxation timescales, $T_2 = 6.9~{\rm d}$ and $T_1 = 144.4~{\rm d}$. The fitted components therefore lie in the fast-transient superradiance regime. Existent VLBI observations motivate the possibility that a single-dish velocity channel blends emission from multiple unresolved flaring regions, although these observations are not used as direct fitting constraints. Although the decomposition is not unique, it provides a physically motivated description of the complex flare morphology within a unified Maxwell-Bloch framework.

title: A Step-Like Transition Underlying the Life and Death of Galaxies
authors: Zhicheng He, Enci Wang, Luis C. Ho, Yingjie Peng, Huiyuan Wang, Yong Shi, Tao Wang, Yongquan Xue, Tinggui Wang
abstract: How galaxies stop forming stars is a complex and central problem in astrophysics. Numerous physical mechanisms have been proposed, yet a simple, unified framework connecting these mechanisms remains lacking. Here, we derive a step-function quenching response from the fundamental principle of gas mass conservation, governed by the competition between gas-supply and gas-depletion timescales. This response also enables the gas-supply timescale to be inferred from the observed quenched fraction. Applying this method to approximately 350,000 galaxies, we find a characteristic gas-supply timescale of ~1 Gyr, reveal distinct inside-out and outside-in quenching signatures associated with supermassive black holes and dark matter halos, respectively, and identify galaxies with intermediate stellar surface mass densities as occupying a critical state for quenching and rejuvenation. Our work establishes a unified physical framework in which a simple step-function response captures how diverse physical processes regulate galaxy quenching and the resumption of star formation through their effects on the competition between gas-supply and gas-depletion timescales.

title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
authors: Bohan Sun, Zunhai Su, Xialie Zhuang, Jianjin Li, Ngai Wong, Chuan-Wei Kuo
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.

title: OLiVES: An Outdoor Low-Light Video Benchmark for Enhancement and Segmentation
authors: Yini Li, Joanne Lin, David Blackham, David Bull, Nantheera Anantrasirichai
abstract: Low-light video processing remains an underexplored problem in computer vision, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality ground-truth data. Existing public datasets exhibit several limitations, including restricted motion diversity, limited scene coverage, weak degradations, reliance on auxiliary modalities such as event data, and misalignment between low-light inputs and ground truth. Furthermore, current datasets typically address either low-light enhancement or scene understanding, whereas these tasks should be considered jointly. We introduce \textbf{OLiVES}, a benchmark dataset for outdoor low-light videos with dynamic scenes, designed to support both low-light video enhancement (LLVE) and video object segmentation (VOS). The dataset addresses key content gaps by incorporating a diverse range of natural textures, animals, occlusions, dynamic activities, and close-up scenes. To the best of our knowledge, OLiVES is the first outdoor low-light video dataset captured using professional cinema-grade cameras. It provides over 25,000 aligned normal- and low-light frame pairs, along with over 46,000 VOS annotations. We benchmark state-of-the-art LLVE and VOS methods on OLiVES and show that training on it improves performance on both tasks. The OLiVES project page is available at: https://anonymous-OLiVES.github.io/.

title: Average-Reward Policy Identification from a Single Continuing Trajectory
authors: Tongxi Wang
abstract: In reinforcement learning, an agent must explore an unknown environment to learn how to make good decisions. Unlike methods that can freely sample any state--action pair, an agent learning from a single trajectory must spend additional time navigating between states. It is therefore natural to expect that learning from a single trajectory requires more experience. In this paper, we show that this additional cost is not always necessary. For average-reward reinforcement learning, we develop an algorithm that learns where to collect information while ensuring that the required samples can be obtained efficiently. We establish an upper bound on the number of interactions needed to identify a near-optimal policy. Furthermore, we prove a matching information theoretic lower bound, showing that, for a broad class of environments and at sufficiently high accuracy, learning from a single trajectory is no harder in the worst case than learning with unrestricted access to state action samples. Our results reveal that the additional complexity cost of navigation can be avoided by adapting information gathering requirements to how the environment provides information.

title: Quantum Spectral Estimation with Multiple Initial States: Improved Error and Cost Scaling
authors: Lingwei Zhang, Zhiyan Ding
abstract: We study quantum spectrum and eigenstate property estimation using multiple initial states and generalized Hadamard tests. Building on the QFAMES (quantum filtering and analysis of multiplicities in eigenvalue spectra) framework, we introduce a new method that samples evolution times independently for each initial-state pair. Under the stated assumptions, when statistical error determines the sampling cost, the total Hamiltonian simulation cost required for fixed-accuracy eigenvalue and observable estimation is independent of the number of initial states, up to logarithmic factors. This improves scalability when many initial states are needed to explore the target eigenspaces. The method also reduces the cost of multiplicity recovery and retains Heisenberg-limited scaling for eigenvalue estimation. Numerical experiments support the predicted statistical error scalings.

title: Lost in Translation: Why Lower Bias Scores Don't Mean Fairer Models
authors: Harsh Kumar
abstract: Bias audits of multilingual language models usually compare a model's average stereotype score in English with its average in another language and read the difference as a difference in fairness. We ask how much of that difference is noise. Auditing ten open models in eight languages, we measure how far scores move when English test items are merely reworded, test every language shift item by item, and check that the test catches shifts we inject on purpose. In all 70 model-language pairs the stereotype score falls below its English level, and for Hindi, Korean and Swahili the drop clearly exceeds what rewording English produces; most of it comes from StereoSet items. Judging every translation, we find that imperfect ones drop more, but faithful translations alone drop nearly as much. Still, a lower average does not show that a model is fairer. An item's English score predicts its translated score far less well than its reworded score (correlation 0.23, 0.27 on faithful translations, vs. 0.48), while scores stay as far from neutral, models agree on translated items, and within Hindi or Spanish a translated item's score correlates with its own rewording at 0.84 and 0.82. The average cannot distinguish lower bias from a different pattern of item-level scores. We also document three common pipeline errors that silently erase bias signal, and release our code.

title: Magnetic Susceptibility of Superconducting Films in the Meissner-London Regime
authors: Ruslan Prozorov
abstract: Extracting the London penetration depth, $λ(T)$, from the measured magnetic susceptibility, $χ(T)$, of a superconducting platelet in a perpendicular magnetic field requires knowing the function $χ(λ)$ computed for the actual sample geometry. Thin films are increasingly important in quantum computing and superconducting electronics, most of which operate at ultra-low excitation fields in the vortex-free regime. Understanding their electromagnetic response in the Meissner--London (finite-$λ$, no vortices) state is therefore essential for extracting intrinsic properties such as the London penetration depth and superfluid phase stiffness. While numerous prior works have addressed different aspects of this problem, here we focus on providing an analytical semi-empirical representation of $χ(λ)$ based on the 2D sheet-current model and establishing the limits of its applicability using two independent full 3D numerical solutions: finite-element modeling and a volume-current integral equation. As a result, we provide $χ(λ)$ for a disc of radius $a$ and thickness $d$ in closed form, valid for all $λ$ and for aspect ratios $δ\equiv d/(2a)\le0.05$, and accurate to $0.1\%$. The two-dimensional sheet description with Pearl length $Λ=2λ^2/d$ is adequate for $δ\lesssim10^{-4}$ and $λ\gtrsim 4d$. Thicker films require the full closed form, which includes the three-dimensional corrections. Using the same numerical analysis, we provide an empirical formula that maps rectangular samples---the geometry most commonly used in experiments---onto a disc with an ``effective radius'' for subsequent calculation of $χ(λ)$, and formulate a complete calibration protocol for whole-sample susceptibility measurements.

title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm
authors: Qianru Meng, Xi Zhang, Konstantinos Papakostas, Congfeng Cao, Wenxiang Hu, Tianyi Lu, Xiao Zhang, Lun Zhou, Zaiqiao Meng, Zhaochun Ren, Xiaohui Yan, Yougang Lyu
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents' research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can combine evidence and implementations from different research directions to guide their agents' subsequent experiments. However, poor experimental results can leave unclear whether to revise a hypothesis or its implementation, while overall program scores can hide components useful to other agents. To address these challenges, we introduce SwarmRSI, a framework that evolves scientific agent swarms for recursive self-improvement. We devise Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation to refine hypotheses and their implementations using experimental feedback from other agents. We also propose Complementary Swarm Recombination to reuse retained hypotheses and complementary program components across agents, allowing partial results to support new research. Recursive Swarm Evolution integrates both mechanisms into a feedback loop, using new experimental evidence to guide subsequent research. Experiments on OpenProblems, NatureBench and MLE-Bench Lite demonstrate SwarmRSI's state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. Further evaluations show that accumulated research experience improves performance on held-out tasks. Biologists also reproduce its programs for follow-up biological analyses.

title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully
authors: Daman Arora, Xuecheng Liu, Himanshu Gaurav Singh, Fahim Tajwar, Abitha Thankaraj, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Haiwen Feng, Yuda Song, Andrea Zanette
abstract: Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully: to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.

title: Relative entropy in quantum field theory: the case of squeezed fermions
authors: Markus B. Fröb
abstract: We review the role of relative entropy in quantum field theories, where the local von Neumann algebras are generically of type III. Consequently, only few exact results are known, and even bounds are difficult to obtain. As a new result, we prove that the relative entropy between a locally squeezed state and the Minkowski vacuum is finite for free fermions.

title: Bounded-Density Vertex Deletion Beyond Vertex Cover
authors: Adrian Miclăuş, Alexandru Popa, Andrei Popa
abstract: We study \textsc{Bounded-Density Vertex Deletion} (BDVD), where one asks whether at most \(k\) vertices can be deleted so that every remaining subgraph has density at most a rational input threshold \(τ_ρ\). We address the twin-cover and distance-to-cluster cases left open by Raupach, Breitkopf, Herrmann, and Nichterlein (MFCS 2026). We prove fixed-parameter tractability parameterized solely by the twin-cover number, for unrestricted input density. For distance to cluster, we establish fixed-parameter tractability parameterized by \(\operatorname{dc}(G)+\lfloor2τ_ρ+1\rfloor\), and complement this with \(\mathsf{W[1]}\)-hardness parameterized by \(\operatorname{dc}(G)\) alone when the target density is part of the input, even for integral targets. Thus distance to cluster alone is fixed-parameter tractable throughout \(τ_ρ<1\), while it is insufficient for unrestricted input density. Finally, we settle the combined parameter treewidth plus solution size, an open problem posed by Bazgan, Nichterlein, and Vazquez Alferez (JCSS 2025). We prove that BDVD is \(\mathsf{W[1]}\)-hard parameterized by \(\operatorname{td}(G)+k\), and hence also by \(\operatorname{tw}(G)+k\), already for targets strictly between \(1\) and \(2\).

title: What Should a Software Team Spend on Agents? Simulation-Based Cost Optimization of Mixed AI-Human Teams
authors: Steffen Herbold
abstract: Context: AI agents are rapidly adopted in software development, but their token costs are rising and it is unclear how much a team should spend on agents, and on which tasks. Objective: We determine how teams should divide spending between human developers and AI agents to deliver the features a project demands at the lowest total cost. Method: We model mixed teams of human developers and AI agents with eight specialized roles as a discrete-time stochastic process covering bug injection and detection, technical debt, human supervision of agents, and release cycles with feature freezes. Using Monte Carlo simulation and evolutionary search, we determine cost-optimal teams for 432 scenarios varying developer capability, project velocity, debt dynamics, agent capability and price, and bug costs, and compare them with a human-only baseline. Results: Escaped bugs are the dominant cost driver, and 61% of the agent budget goes to finding bugs. Agent capability matters more than token price, since higher-quality outputs reduce downstream quality assurance costs. In teams with capable agents, human developers mostly fix bugs and leave the implementation of new features to the agents. Teams with high-capability agents are typically cheaper than human-only teams, but low-capability agents offer no consistent advantage. At realistic velocities, the optimal teams still spend more on developers than on agents. Conclusions: There is neither a universal token budget per developer nor a universal agentic team structure. As in traditional development, this depends on many factors and teams need to be carefully tailored to the project context to achieve the optimal cost-quality trade-off.

title: Probing Planet Formation within 10 au: Dust Substructures in Extremely Compact Protoplanetary Disks
authors: Pietro Curone, Gijs D. Mulders, Nienke van der Marel, Laura M. Pérez
abstract: ALMA high-resolution surveys have so far focused mainly on large, bright protoplanetary disks, where substructures are routinely detected, leaving compact disks poorly characterized. Yet, the survival of millimeter emission in Class II sources implies that radial drift must have been halted by pressure traps, previously undetected due to limited angular resolution. We present ALMA Band 7 (0.9 mm) continuum observations of 11 of the smallest ($R_{68} < 10$ au) Class II disks in Lupus, reaching $0.02''$ (2 au) resolution, the highest currently available with ALMA at this wavelength. We detect substructures in 4 disks, including a clear inner cavity of radius 1.6 au, and hints of substructure in 3 more. Two disks also host faint outer rings beyond their bright inner core. Combining these results with demographic information on Class II disks observed with ALMA, we examine how the substructure detection rate varies with disk size, restricting to disks whose diameter is resolved by at least 3 resolution elements. We find that nearly all disks ($\gtrsim$95%) larger than 30 au show substructures, compared to a still substantial $\sim$50% between 3 and 30 au, with the lower rate likely affected by optical depth. The planet masses required to open gaps within 5 au fall in the super-Earth to mini-Neptune regime. These results demonstrate that substructures are ubiquitous across the disk population, and that planet formation conditions can be probed down to a few au from the host star.

title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Xiao Yang
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.

title: Modeling Diffuse Scattering in Mobility Scenarios: Ray Tracing Model and Measurement Validation
authors: Milica Djordjevic, Thomas Wilding, Anja Dakić, Markus Hofer, Benjamin Rainer, Thomas Zemen
abstract: Open-source ray tracing (RT) frameworks are increasingly used for site-specific channel modeling due to their reproducibility and extensibility. In non-stationary mobility scenarios, repeated RT evaluations can generate different diffuse propagation paths without preserving their correspondence, limiting a consistent representation of their temporal evolution. To address this limitation, we extend diffuse scattering modeling in Sionna RT using persistent surface-associated scattering points. Their positions remain fixed, while their contributions evolve according to changes in the propagation geometry and visibility. The proposed approach is validated using empirical radio channel impulse response measurements in an urban vehicular scenario at 5.9 GHz. Compared with the standard Sionna RT baseline, the proposed model shows improved agreement with measurements in the delay and Doppler domains.

title: Hypothesis Selection via Weighted Medians
authors: Liang-Yu Zou
abstract: Given $n$ distributions (hypotheses) $\mathcal H=\{H_1,\ldots,H_n\}$ and samples from an unknown target distribution $P$, proper hypothesis selection seeks a distribution whose total variation distance to $P$ is close to the best achievable within the known distributions. We give an algorithm that, using $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ target samples, running in $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ time, with probability at least $1-δ$, returns $H_{\hat i}$ satisfying $d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_{\hat i})\leq 3\min_{i\in[n]}d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_i)+\varepsilon.$ The algorithm achieves the optimal approximation factor and sample complexity. The running time improves the dependence on the failure probability from polynomial to logarithmic in the state-of-the-art bound $\tilde{O}(n\varepsilon^{-2}δ^{-1})$ of Aamand, Aliakbarpour, Chen, and Silwal (COLT 2026), thereby answering their Question~2.

title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient
authors: Yu-Xuan Shi, Mingze Ma, Xi Chen
