We develop a distributional framework for the resulting dynamics and give them a finite-dimensional meaning through projections onto statistical manifolds. We identify the true background as the unique zero of a limiting generalized gradient and, under suitable stability, compactness, integrability and approximation conditions, establish a conditional consistency theorem for measurable estimators satisfying the empirical projected equations on events whose probabilities tend to one. Finally, we specialize the construction to Gaussian-mixture manifolds and obtain an explicit finite-dimensional scheme.

title: Decay-Ramsey Sequences
authors: Francesco Di Braccio, Simon Griffiths, Pedram Noohi, Leo Versteegen
abstract: Given a sequence $\mathbf{a}=(a_i)_{i\geq 1}$ of positive real numbers, we say that a colouring $c:E(K_n)\to \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbf{a}$-bounded if the proportion of edges coloured $i$ is at most $a_i$, for all $i$. We write \[ \mathbf{a}\, \to\, K_k \] if, for all sufficiently large $n$, all $\mathbf{a}$-bounded colourings $c:E(K_n)\to \mathbb{N}$ contain a monochromatic $K_k$. We say that the sequence $\mathbf{a}$ is \emph{Decay-Ramsey} if $\mathbf{a}\to K_k$ for all $k\ge 2$. In this short paper we introduce the question of determining which sequences are Decay-Ramsey and present some initial results.

title: Designing Hamiltonians with Exactly Flat Higher-Vortexable Bands
authors: Daniel Spasic-Mlacak, Nigel R. Cooper
abstract: The zero modes of the Aharonov-Casher Hamiltonian form an exactly flat, vortexable Chern band in any nonuniform magnetic field, analogous to the lowest Landau level. We ask which local Hamiltonians host exactly flat higher-vortexable bands. For a scalar Hamiltonian, an exactly flat first-vortexable band requires a mass proportional to the local field; the Dirac analogue has the same structure. For periodic Bernal bilayer graphene with nonzero mean flux, the exact zero-mode pair is genuinely first-vortexable if and only if the interlayer hopping has nonzero mean; zero-mean hopping instead gives a decomposable pair. Multiorbital models yield exact higher-vortexable chains to arbitrary order, while remaining first order in momentum.

title: Quantization of positive Lagrangians
authors: Jake P. Solomon, Bentzion Yavetz
abstract: A Lagrangian submanifold in an almost Calabi-Yau manifold is called positive if the real part of the holomorphic volume form restricted to it is positive. It is called $ε$-positive if the ratio of the restrictions of the imaginary and real parts of the holomorphic volume form is bounded by $\frac{1}ε.$ An exact isotopy class of positive Lagrangian submanifolds admits a natural Riemannian metric. We prove that the Riemannian metric restricted to the subset of $ε$-positive Lagrangians induces a path metric when the relative Kähler class of the ambient Calabi-Yau manifold lies on a line of rational slope. The proof relies on the construction of a sequence of quantization maps from a circle bundle over the space of positive Lagrangians to the dual of the space of holomorphic sections of powers of a prequantum line bundle. The rationality condition for the relative Kähler class allows us to reduce to the case of Bohr-Sommerfeld Lagrangians. Building on ideas of Tian and Nirenberg-Wells, Hörmander estimates are used to show that functions on a Bohr-Sommerfeld Lagrangian can be approximated by holomorphic sections of a sufficiently high power of the prequantum line bundle. Consequently, the quantization maps eventually separate fibers of the circle bundle.

title: Simultaneous Secure Communications and Sensing Privacy with Full Duplex MIMO Radios
authors: Ioannis Gavras, George C. Alexandropoulos
abstract: This paper proposes a Full Duplex (FD) framework for safeguarding Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) against a passive multi-antenna Eavesdropper (Eve). The adversary is modeled as both a communication and sensing threat, seeking to decode uplink data streams and estimate the surrounding scene. Eve's threat is quantified through two worst-case requirements over a location uncertainty region: a minimum secrecy rate for data confidentiality and a minimum eavesdropping Cramer-Rao Bound (CRB) for sensing privacy. We derive the eavesdropping information measures governing both data interception and scene inference, showcasing that transmitting Artificial Noise (AN) can degrade Eve's capabilities through the inverse interference-plus-noise covariance. Exploiting the underlying structure of the problem, we characterize finite-power local and robust feasibility conditions for target secrecy-privacy pairs. The analysis showcases that AN is fundamentally subspace-limited: increasing power is beneficial only along Eve's communication channel and sensing-derivative directions illuminated by the effective AN subspace. Finally, we formulate an AN power allocation problem that is solved via monotone branch-and-bound, and numerical evaluations quantify the AN power required to guarantee joint secrecy and sensing privacy.

title: Quantum Work Statistics from Entanglement-Assisted Invariance
authors: Akira Sone, Akram Touil, Emery Doucet, Sebastian Deffner
abstract: We demonstrate that the one-time measurement scheme is more consistent than the standard two-time measurement scheme with respect to the fundamental symmetry of entanglement, namely entanglement-assisted invariance (envariance). In particular, the work statistics obtained from the one-time measurement scheme arise naturally as a direct consequence of envariance for any driving unitary, without involving an explicit measurement postulate, whereas the analogous identification for the two-time measurement scheme is possible only for a Haar-measure-zero set of unitaries. This envariance-based formulation eliminates the ambiguity in work statistics related to the energetic cost of measurement.

title: Quantized slow blowup dynamics for the energy-critical Schrödinger map flow
authors: Jacek Jendrej, Jitao Xu, Xu Yuan, Lifeng Zhao
abstract: We study the Cauchy problem for the energy-critical Schrödinger map into the 2-sphere: \[ \partial_{t}u = u\timesΔu, \quad (t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{1+2}, \quad u(t,x)\in\mathbb{S}^2 \] for equivariant initial data of homotopy degree $k=1$. Given any integer $L\in\mathbb{N}_+$, we exhibit a set of initial data arbitrarily close to the ground state harmonic map in the energy norm such that the corresponding solution blows up in finite time with a quantized rate \[ λ(t)\sim \frac{\left(T-t\right)^L}{\left|\log(T-t)\right|^{\frac{2L}{2L-1}}} \quad\mbox{as}\ \ t\uparrow T. \] Our proof is inspired by the techniques developed for the energy-critical harmonic map heat flow in a similar context by Rapha{ë}l and Schweyer~[Anal. PDE 7 (2014), 1713--1805]. However, its adaptation to a Schrödinger-type equation requires the introduction of a new energy-Virial-Morawetz Lyapunov functional tailored to quantized slow blowup dynamics.

title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
authors: Julia Barth, Armin Sommer, Kunvar Thaman, Jannik Schilling
abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.

title: Radion/Dilaton portal freeze-in dark matter in extra-dimensional theories
authors: Amrita Mukherjee, George Sanamyan, Dipan Sengupta
abstract: We perform a comprehensive analysis of a radion/dilaton portal freeze-in dark matter in models of stabilized warped extra-dimensions. We show that the relic abundance of a generic dark matter particle (scalars, vectors, or fermions) is obtained via the conformal coupling of the radial mode in a consistent model stabilized warped extra- dimensions; our calculations show that in scenarios where the reheating temperature is much smaller than the radion mass, keV-TeV scale dark matter particles can saturate the relic density. We perform a comprehensive analysis of a radion/dilaton portal freeze-in dark matter in models of stabilized warped extra-dimensions. We show that the relic abundance of a generic dark matter particle (scalars, vectors, or fermions) is obtained via the conformal coupling of the radial mode in a consistent model stabilized warped extra- dimensions; our calculations show that in scenarios where the reheating temperature is much smaller than the radion mass, keV-TeV scale dark matter particles can saturate the relic density. Furthermore, we show that the model is subject to Lyman-alpha constraints in the keV-GeV range, providing a unique, model-independent probe of this sector. Our calculations extend previous attempts to calculate the freeze-in relic abundance in extra-dimensional portals by providing a consistent theoretical calculation of matrix elements, clearly laying out the underlying motivation and assumptions and providing a comprehensive account of the cosmological constraints on the model.

title: Tidal deformability of white dwarfs in Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity
authors: Santanu Pradhan, Tapobrata Sarkar
abstract: We compute the static quadrupole Love number $k_2$ and the dimensionless tidal deformability $Λ$ of cold white dwarfs in Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld (EiBI) gravity. Matter couples to the physical metric while perturbation equations are solved in an auxiliary metric, so the physical tidal field near the surface depends on derivatives of the equation of state. This dependence is regular for a surface polytropic index $1<Γ_{\rm env}<3/2$, but not for the $Γ= 5/3$ Chandrasekhar equation of state. The mechanism, an algebraic map between the metric that carries perturbations and the metric that matter feels, is common to Palatini-type theories, so the same type of surface condition should apply to tidal calculations in this wider class. We use thermodynamically consistent envelopes that exactly reach zero enthalpy. At five masses from \(0.6\) to \(1.3\,\Msun\) and five sampled Born-Infeld couplings \(κ\), with $|κ|\le5\times10^6\,\mathrm{m^2}$, the EiBI-GR differences are approximately linear in $κ$. The largest absolute fractional shifts are \(3.89\times 10^{-5}\) in the stellar radius $R$, \(4.09\times 10^{-5}\) in $k_2$, and \(2.36\times 10^{-4}\) in $Λ$. Across nine envelope models, half the spread of each quantity relative to the baseline envelope is at most \(0.0186\) in $R$ and \(0.0857\) in \(k_2\), but only \(3.02\times 10^{-5}\) in \(Λ\) as the changes in \(k_2\) and \(R^5\) largely cancel. A high-precision calculation shows that the envelope dependence of the EiBI-GR difference in \(Λ\) is small. Half the spread of this difference ranges from \(1.067\times 10^{-12}\) to \(6.208\times 10^{-11}\) over the 20 nonzero mass-coupling points.

title: A VR Training System for Robot-Assisted Vascular Intervention with Dual-Mode Control and Model-Based Interaction Response
authors: Yining Shang, Shuxiang Guo, Sheng Cao, Pengcheng Li, Bin Wang, Mingchao Ding
abstract: Virtual reality training for robot-assisted vascular intervention requires accurate robotic control and effective feedback on guidewire--vessel interactions. This paper presents a VR training system combining asynchronous dual-mode command mapping with sensorless interaction estimation. The system supports velocity-controlled navigation and position-driven incremental manipulation. Guidewire deformation and a Hunt--Crossley-type contact response are combined and temporally filtered to estimate interaction intensity, while trajectory-based visualization supports post-procedure review. Tests confirmed distinct command-dispatch patterns across three velocity gears and the position mode. During hybrid-scene navigation, the estimated response remained low during straight insertion and increased as the guidewire bent within the vascular model. Trajectory analysis yielded a model-derived cumulative trauma work (CTW) value of 15.166 in normalized units and localized regions of elevated interaction. In a preliminary study with 15 novices, physical-phantom task success increased from 53.3% to 93.3% after VR training, while mean completion time decreased from 132.4 s to 96.7 s. These results demonstrate the system's dual-mode operation, deformation-sensitive feedback, and potential to improve subsequent physical-phantom task performance.

title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
authors: Oscar Chew, Po-Yi Lu, Yi-Jie Cheng, Kunal Jain, Hsuan-Tien Lin, Zhengzhong Tu, Kuan-Hao Huang
abstract: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

title: Binary-lens amplification of starlight: from magnification flares to quasi-periodic tracking of orbital evolution
authors: Hanxi Wang, Bence Kocsis, Miguel Zumalacárregui
abstract: Supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHB) are expected at the center of galaxies as a result of galaxy mergers. The dynamics and evolution of SMBHBs shed light on the evolution and formation of galaxies, the gravitational wave background and the nature of gravity. Many methods have been proposed to identify sub-parsec SMBHBs via the detection of gravitational waves or the modulation of the emission from the surrounding gaseous environment. In a previous study, we proposed a new method of identifying SMBHBs in non-active galactic nuclei via gravitational lensing. The caustics, i.e. the source positions with a divergent magnification, exhibit a complex extended geometry which rotates with the binary period. Each caustic-crossing produces an extreme magnification by up to a factor of $10^{6}$. In this work, we generalize the previous study and describe the rich phenomenology of binary-lens amplification of starlight (BLAST). We explore the electromagnetic transients produced when accounting for the relative proper motion of the source, either a single or a binary star, the eccentricity and precession of the SMBHB, and the relative inclination. Systems where a star rapidly drifts across the caustic produce a single- or double-peaked flare. In the opposite limit, a star with no relative proper motion produces quasi-periodic lensed starlight (QPLS), i.e., repeated peaks that track the system's orbital evolution. We determine the expected magnification and peak duration in different circumstances, and calculate the magnification curves and their Fourier transforms. This study may help construct search pipelines to identify SMBHBs in electromagnetic time-domain surveys.

title: Potatoes and Onions
authors: Marcin Briański, Meike Hatzel, Karolina Okrasa, Michał Pilipczuk
abstract: The first major step in the theory of graph minors of Robertson and Seymour was the grid theorem, a fundamental duality result describing that any graph of sufficiently high treewidth must contain a large grid as a minor. Since this pioneering work, multiple grid theorems have been established in structural graph theory, linking various width parameters of combinatorial objects with the non-existence of grid-like obstructions. In particular, Kawarabayashi and Kreutzer [STOC'15] proved a variant of the grid theorem for directed graphs that links directed treewidth with the non-existence of topological minors of large cylindrical walls. On the other hand, to study immersions of undirected graphs $-$ another containment relation that focuses on edge-disjointness, rather than vertex-disjointness $-$ Wollan [JCTB'15] introduced a parameter, tree-cutwidth, and proved that it is dual to immersions of large walls. In this work, we present a version of Wollan's parameter for directed graphs, the directed tree-cutwidth. The main result is a grid theorem for directed tree-cutwidth, establishing that it is dual to directed immersions of large cylindrical walls.

title: Almost-global convergence to twisted states in discrete Huygens rings
authors: Jorge Buescu, Henrique M. Oliveira
abstract: We study the discrete Huygens phase map on the ring $C_n$, the simplest oscillator network in which the coupling can be frustrated. Reciprocal coupling favours phase opposition between neighbours, while the edge phase differences must sum to zero modulo $2π$ around the cycle; for odd $n$ these two requirements are incompatible. The parity of $n$ determines the absolute minima of the potential. When $4\mid n$, the critical set also contains circles of critical points, all of which meet at two completely degenerate configurations. After quotienting by the common phase, the map is a gradient step for an intrinsic potential on an $(n-1)$-torus, and the cycle spectrum gives an explicit interval of interaction strengths on which every orbit converges to a critical point. Our main result is that, on this whole interval and for every $n\ge3$, almost every orbit converges to a uniform twisted minimum, including at interaction strengths for which the map is not invertible. When $4\mid n$, the non-minimal points of the critical circles are treated by a centre-stable manifold argument. At the two degenerate intersections, a local blow-up reduces the problem to the cubic leading term of the potential and its restriction to the unit sphere. Orbits approaching along directions where this restriction is positive form a null set, because the cubic is harmonic in the intrinsic metric. No orbit approaches along its zero level, where the critical points are non-degenerate saddles on invariant rays. Hence the degenerate equilibria also have basins of zero measure.

title: Improved Precipitation Variability in the Community Atmosphere Model through Implementation of a Neural-Network Deep Convection Scheme
authors: Xavier J. Levine, Griffin Mooers, Jack W. Atkinson, Marat F. Khairoutdinov, Janni Yuval, Dominic Orchard, Paul A. O'Gorman
abstract: Conventional deep convection schemes remain a primary source of uncertainty in global climate models, yet replacing them with data-driven alternatives while maintaining physical consistency and numerical stability is an open challenge. We present a hybrid configuration of the Community Atmosphere Model version 6 (CAM6), in which a fully connected deep neural network replaces the Zhang-McFarlane deep convection scheme (ZM), while radiation, turbulence, and other cloud processes are left unchanged. The network is trained on output from a storm-resolving global model - the global System for Atmospheric Modeling (gSAM) - using a coarse-graining approach to derive subgrid-scale convective fluxes and tendencies. This data-driven parameterization is ported to CAM6 and found to run stably for more than a decade while conserving energy and moisture. It produces a broadly realistic climatology without retuning the remaining parameterizations. Relative to the default Zhang-McFarlane scheme, the neural network parameterization substantially improves some long-standing model deficiencies. In particular, the biases in light precipitation and extreme precipitation are markedly reduced, and the diurnal cycle of tropical land precipitation shifts from a spurious midday peak over many regions to the observed late-afternoon peak. These results support targeted ML-based convection schemes as a viable path toward reducing systematic model errors in next-generation climate models.

title: The Sum of All Summaries: PROPALIGN for Graded Proposition Salience Evaluation
authors: Lin Ai, Emma Thronson, Katherine Conhaim, Amir Zeldes
abstract: Identification and ranking of salient propositions in documents is indirectly involved in many AI tasks, but few papers define proposition salience scores clearly, make diverse data available, or evaluate models directly on the task. This paper proposes PROPALIGN, a multiple-summary-based approach for propositional salience score estimation, and releases PROPALIGNBANK, an accompanying dataset for the method with 138K alignments of over 35K propositions. We compare several approaches to salient proposition extraction in English across a broad range of spoken and written genres, and demonstrate that naively asking models for judgments leads to inconsistencies. By contrast, graded, summary-based metrics are more stable. We further observe that while single models perform worse than humans, an ensemble of models incorporating linguistic features approaches manual annotation quality ceilings. In addition, analyses of the model outputs suggest insights into how models can extract salient information with and without the use of summaries.

title: Hypergraphs with the smallest Hall ratio are still hard to colour
authors: Veronica Bitonti, Freddie Illingworth, Pedram Noohi, Jane Tan
abstract: For $H$ a hypergraph, the Hall ratio $ρ(H)=\text{max}_{X\subseteq V(H)}\frac{\lvert{X}\rvert}{α(H[X])}$ is a natural lower bound for its chromatic number, and among non-empty $k$-uniform hypergraphs the smallest possible Hall ratio is $k/(k-1)$. For graphs ($k = 2$), having minimum Hall ratio $2$ forces chromatic number $2$. Nešetřil, Rödl, and Sales asked whether a similar phenomenon holds at higher uniformities. We answer this question negatively in a strong form, showing that for every $k \geqslant 3$ there are $k$-uniform hypergraphs with Hall ratio exactly $k/(k-1)$ and arbitrarily large fractional chromatic number.

title: Bouncing Bianchi Type I Universes with Interacting Vacuum
authors: Marco Bruni, Rodrigo Maier, Thomas Waters
abstract: We investigate the global dynamics and cosmological viability of non-singular solutions in an anisotropic Bianchi type I universe featuring an interacting vacuum energy component $V$ and a perfect fluid $ρ$, extending previous work based on a Robertson-Walker geometry. By modeling the energy-momentum transfer via a phenomenological four-vector $Q_μ$, we reduce the field equations to a four-dimensional autonomous dynamical system for the expansion rate $Θ$, total shear $σ$, energy density $ρ$, and vacuum component $V$. We examine two distinct forms for how the interaction depends on $ρ$ and $V$: a linear coupling $Q_1 \propto Θ[ξ(V_Λ- V) + χρ]$ and a non-linear coupling $Q_2 \propto Θρ(1 - V/V_Λ)$. Using a potential-energy analogy and phase-space analysis, we show that the linear model $Q_1$ naturally admits non-singular bouncing trajectories. In contrast, unlike the Robertson-Walker case, for the non-linear interaction $Q_2$, invariant boundary surfaces in phase space strictly constrain the domain of expansion ruling out cosmological bounce scenarios for physical matter configurations.

title: Beyond Expert Rankings: Contrast Calibration for Mixed-Precision MoE Quantization
authors: Renjie Xie, Juncheng Yang, Aoting Hu, Yan Liang, Mingxi Zhang, Zheheng Hong, Wei Xu, Yanzhi Chen
abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models activate only a few experts per token, yet all expert weights must be stored. Mixed-precision quantization reduces this storage cost by assigning higher bit-widths to sensitive experts and lower bit-widths to resilient ones, but expert rankings alone do not determine how strongly to weight their errors. To address this gap, we propose NatScale, a contrast-calibrated allocation framework for mixed-precision MoE quantization. It uses a model-specific power transformation to calibrate gradient-based expert weights to an information-theoretic contrast target while preserving rankings. We jointly evaluate each expert's gate, up and down configurations to estimate its output error. We then combine these errors and calibrated weights with an existing prior based on weight spectra, variance and precision decay to select configurations under a storage budget. Across three models, NatScale achieves the lowest native-to-quantized KL divergence and the highest top-token agreement in all nine settings against five allocation baselines. It also yields the lowest perplexity in seven settings. These findings highlight the importance of objective-aware precision allocation.

title: InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views
authors: Yongzhen Hu, Hao Yu, Jiawei Wang, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Xingliang Liu, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou, Hujun Bao, Sida Peng
abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction builds 3D scenes directly from input images for novel view rendering, but learning Gaussian attributes from predicted geometry for high-quality rendering under large viewpoint changes remains challenging. We analyze limitations in Gaussian attribute learning and introduce InfiniSplat v2, which improves rendering quality through architectural and training changes. Our method decouples geometry and attribute prediction with a frozen geometry branch, aligns predicted Gaussians using ground-truth camera poses during training, and adopts large-angle target view supervision. Across six datasets, the feed-forward outputs of the same trained model achieve state-of-the-art mean LPIPS and DISTS among the evaluated methods in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings. In the pose-conditioned setting, mean LPIPS and DISTS decrease by 25.8% and 32.9%, respectively, compared with the strongest evaluated baselines. We further find that opacity learned with only image reconstruction supervision suppresses geometrically inconsistent points. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/InfiniSplat2/

title: Training Dynamics of Transformers on Unbounded Inputs: Attention Learning Can Lag Output Layer Learning
authors: Yaomengxi Han, Debarghya Ghoshdastidar
abstract: The success of transformers is attributed to several factors, including their capacity to express formal languages over variable-length inputs, and ability of the attention mechanism to focus on relevant input features. However, there is limited understanding of the training dynamics of shallow transformers, specifically how to decouple the learning of the attention and the output (feedforward) layer. A natural extension of the theory of one-step gradient feature learning in feedforward networks suggests that one could first learn the attention weights with a single gradient step, and then train the output layer. We show that this fails for a shallow transformer trained to recognize a star-free language from unbounded-length input. We prove that the transformer can be trained to recognize the language with a three-phase gradient descent: the output layer is updated first, followed by an attention update, and the output layer is fine-tuned in the third phase. In contrast, the language cannot be learned by training only the attention or output layer, or by a single attention-layer update followed by finetuning the output layer. We empirically show that ``attention learning lagging output layer learning" is beneficial in other language recognition, regression, and in-context learning tasks as well.

title: AutoRSR: Automated Real-to-Sim-to-Real Data Generation for Scalable Robot Learning
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Chang Liu, Litao Deng, Tao Zhang, Qin Jin
abstract: Scaling embodied robot learning requires large and diverse manipulation datasets, but collecting real-world demonstrations remains expensive in human effort and robot time. Simulation provides a scalable alternative, yet converting a real workspace into a robot-learning-ready environment still requires substantial manual effort for object extraction, asset processing, coordinate calibration, and trajectory specification. We present AutoRSR, a highly automated real-to-sim-to real framework that converts scanned real-world workspaces into reusable embodied simulation assets and scalable manipulation data. Given multi-view observations, robot states, and open-vocabulary semantic queries, AutoRSR reconstructs the workspace, extracts individual object assets, and automatically registers the reconstructed scene to the robot base frame at metric scale. Starting from a small number of reference motions, AutoRSR then generates executable manipulation trajectories and scales them through trajectory interpolation and domain randomization. After workspace scanning and semantic queries, the remaining pipeline requires no manual object annotation, scene-to-robot calibration, or robot teleoperation. Across three real-world manipulation tasks, policies trained on 1K automatically generated episodes per task achieve 73.3--86.7% real-world success rates, comparable to pi 0.5 trained from 150 human teleoperated demonstrations, while reducing the human time required for data generation by an order of magnitude. These results demonstrate that real-world observations can be converted into metrically aligned, executable, and scalable simulation data with substantially reduced human effort.

title: Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation
authors: Yuheng Chen, Yufan Chen, Zhuojun Cai, Ruiping Liu, Junwei Zheng, Jiale Wei, Di Wen, Weijia Fan, Kunyu Peng, Jiaming Zhang, Rainer Stiefelhagen
abstract: Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yufanchen96/RPD

title: Argument Graph Uncertainty: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Logical Structure of Reasoning Chains
authors: Simon Baur, Sumire Honda, Wojciech Samek, Jackie Ma
abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for deploying large language models in high-stakes reasoning tasks, yet most existing approaches rely on expensive sampling strategies or shallow token-level signals that ignore the internal logical structure of model outputs. We introduce Argument Graph Uncertainty, a post-hoc framework for multiple choice question tasks, that estimates model confidence directly from the logical structure of a single chain-of-thought reasoning trace. Our method uses either a lightweight instruction-tuned model or a simple deterministic rule to segment the reasoning chain into propositional units, then applies a NLI model to infer relational edges and construct two complementary argument graphs over these segments. The resulting edge scores are aggregated into a Dirichlet posterior over answer options, whose concentration yields calibrated uncertainty estimates reflecting both local step-to-step coherence and global logical consistency across the reasoning trace. Evaluated on GPQA, MMLU-Pro and TruthfulQA, our method consistently surpasses token-based and consistency-based uncertainty baselines across multiple reasoning models. We further demonstrate through extensive combination analyses that argument graph uncertainty captures an orthogonal signal to existing approaches, making it a complementary component in uncertainty ensembles. Crucially, our framework requires no additional calls to the evaluated model and relies entirely on small, efficient auxiliary models, producing fully interpretable, per-node uncertainty attributions at low computational cost.

title: Anuvani-Diarization: Zero Shot Speaker Diarization and Annotation Conventions Across 22 Languages
authors: Stephen Fernandes, Narayan Choudhary
abstract: India's 22 scheduled languages are spoken by over a billion people in conversations that mix languages, often within one turn, overlap freely, and take place over telephones, in meetings, and in media. Knowing who spoke when, the task of speaker diarization, is essential to speech applications for such conversation: voice agents conversing with several people at once, speaker attributed transcription of meetings and calls, contact center analytics, and media monitoring. We present a systematic study of speaker diarization across all 22 languages on IndicDiarBench and introduce Anuvani-Diarization, which adapts a self-supervised end-to-end segmentation model to Indian conversation with uncertainty aware silver supervision. Evaluated zero shot alongside nine recent diarization systems, it reaches a duration weighted diarization error rate (DER) of 16.78% on all 1,164 recordings, the lowest of all systems we ran and second only to the best published result (16.0%), and leads the three strongest rivals in 14 of 22 languages. It matches its parent on six international benchmarks. We also show that the benchmark's utterance level annotation convention is a hidden variable worth 1.9 to 4.1 DER points, depending on the system, and that a convention learned from other Indian transcriptions does not transfer.

title: Cache-Aided Linear Function Computation
authors: Xiaohong Cai, Ruze Zhang, Laigang Guo, Raymond W. Yeung
abstract: We study cache-aided linear computation in distributed systems where each source generates and stores its own data. An external receiver requests a linear combination of these data, and the sources use information cached before the request is known to reduce the communication needed to recover the requested result. In our model, each of the $N$ sources stores its own independent file over a finite field and has an additional cache of normalized size $M$. The receiver must recover any requested linear combination with zero error from the messages sent by the sources over separate noiseless links. We establish a lower bound on the worst-case communication rate over any finite field by analyzing several requests under the same cache placement. This bound determines the optimal rate when no additional cache is available. For binary files, we propose parity-aided placement (PAP), a coded-placement scheme that combines cached parities with uncoded symbols. For every $N\geq3$, we characterize its communication rate for each request and optimize its placement parameters to obtain a closed-form worst-case rate. The resulting achievable rate meets the lower bound for $0\leq M\leq1/(2N-1)$ and $M\geq(N-1)/N$, establishing the optimal memory--rate tradeoff in these two ranges.

title: Beyond Static Cues: Unified Dynamic Detection of MLLM Backdoors via Dual-Flow Trajectory Analysis
authors: Yinzhen Huang, Jiahe Xie, Yitong Sun, Ruochen Zhang, Xingxing Wei
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, yet their susceptibility to backdoor attacks remains a formidable challenge. While existing defenses have evolved from visual-centric patch cues to unsupervised internal attention statistics, they are fundamentally constrained by a reliance on static snapshots and attack-specific heuristics. Given the intricate interplay between dual modalities, the vast design space for multimodal triggers allows diverse threats, such as textual injections, sub-perceptual noises, and coordinated cross-modal triggers, to easily circumvent such rigid priors, particularly when attack types are unknown in real-world applications. In this paper, we rethink backdoor detection by shifting the diagnostic paradigm from static observations to dynamic output evolution. We observe that a successful attack inevitably hijacks the model's decoding trajectory, skewing internal modal contributions during generation while maintaining an abnormal output invariance despite input perturbations. To capture this behavior, we propose EVO-Detect, a unified detection framework that monitors the dynamic evolution of internal signals during early decoding steps through two complementary channels: Attention Flow and Logits Flow. The attention branch measures how image-text attention allocation evolves during early generation, whereas the logits branch quantifies the sensitivity of the output distribution to modal perturbations through interventional ablations. We then convert these trajectories into compact sample-level metrics and normalize them against negative-control signatures so that natural perturbations are less likely to be mistaken for backdoor evidence. Extensive evaluations show that our approach substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines such as BYE and TCAP across diverse attack families.

title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation For Robot Policies
authors: Motasem Alfarra, Pietro Mazzaglia, Markus Peschl, Daniel Dijkman, Christos Louizos
abstract: Reinforcement-learning policies for robot locomotion can fail at deployment when operating conditions shift (e.g., rough or slippery terrain, payload changes, sensing degradation), and retraining or manual recalibration is often infeasible under on-device latency and memory constraints. We study test-time adaptation (TTA) for robotic control: adapting a pretrained policy online and in a self-supervised manner during execution, without access to rewards. Our starting point is a lightweight baseline that updates only the actor using a frozen pretrained critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate. Building on this, we introduce TEMPO, a test-time entropy-regularized, memory-guided policy optimization method that stabilizes critic-driven updates under severe shift. TEMPO combines (i) an entropy-promoting regularizer on the critic's predictive distribution to mitigate overconfident extrapolation, and (ii) a score-based memory, inspired by prioritized replay, that prioritizes low-value ("hard") observations and applies importance sampling to focus limited computation on the most informative deployment conditions. Across Go1, Go2, and G1 in MuJoCo Playground under four representative shifts and multiple architectures, TEMPO yields consistent gains, reaching up to 80% improvement in a single-device setting. We further validate on a physical Unitree Go2 with an added calf payload, where fully on-device adaptation improves performance over the non-adapted baseline across real-world episodes.

title: Reflect After Failure: Brain-Inspired Self-Evolving Agents for Embodied Spatial Intelligence
authors: Xin Li, Xiaohuan Gu, Yifan Wang, Shaobin Ling, Tianli Shi, Jingao Xu, Zhimeng Yin, Dapeng Wu, Yun Wang
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have made substantial progress in spatial reasoning, and self-evolving agents further extend these capabilities to embodied environments by learning from interactions. However, current self-evolution remains particularly challenging in embodied spatial tasks, complex and multi-step decisions from partial visual evidence making it difficult to determine why an execution fails. The failure may stem from misperception, insufficient exploration, or incorrect planning, yet execution feedback alone rarely reveals which component is responsible. As a result, simply accumulating interaction experience can reinforce ineffective strategies. To address this, we propose HiMeco, a brain-inspired self-evolving agent for embodied spatial intelligence, inspired by metacognitive monitoring and hippocampal memory consolidation. Through Hippocampal-Metacognitive Reflection, HiMeco diagnoses failures in perception-exploration-planning (PEP), then compares execution attempts to derive reusable strategies and guidance for avoiding recurring errors. It also abstracts interaction programs into parameterized skills, using evidence contracts and execution-based validation to determine their retention and reuse. These strategies and skills guide subsequent interactions, with memory updated only between rounds and model parameters kept frozen. HiMeco achieves state-of-the-art performance on ESI-Bench, and it also improves accuracy on EmbSpatial-Bench by 3.94 percentage points without evolution.

title: Event Cameras versus Frame Cameras for Synthetic-Aperture Imaging: A Simulation Study
authors: Jakob Hinterholzer, Mohamed Youssef, Oliver Bimber
abstract: Synthetic-aperture imaging (SAI) removes occluders such as foliage by integrating many views of a scene along a camera path. It has so far been used mainly with frame cameras. We ask whether an event camera has advantages for SAI, and answer the question in simulation, where both sensors see exactly the same scene and the same camera movement. A densely rendered Blender sequence is turned into frames with an EMVA~1288 noise model of an industrial global-shutter camera, and into an event stream with the v2e simulator parameterized like a Sony IMX636. The frames are integrated with the existing airborne optical sectioning renderer. For the events we add a new integration path that projects every single event onto the focal plane at its own interpolated pose, so no events have to be binned into frames. We compare the two sensors in three main runs and an additional dark high-speed test. In a bright scene at 25,m/s the frame camera records only three images on the path and cannot remove the occluder, while the event camera reconstructs the target, even after an event-rate controller drops most of its events to fit the camera link. At the same speed in a 5,lux scene the event camera no longer resolves the target either. In a 5,lux scene at 5,m/s both sensors reconstruct the target at similar quality. We also compare the data one traversal of the aperture costs. At high speed the capped event stream still shows the target at the same data volume as the three frames. At 1,m/s we compare both cameras at two matched data budgets, and there the event camera has no advantage over the frame camera in reconstruction quality. The data rate of the event camera depends on the scene and is highest exactly in the fast bright scenes where it is needed most.

title: Taking the PULSE of Medical Reasoning: Step-Level Retrieval Timing for Knowledge-Grounded Inference
authors: Danyang Zhao, Sendong Zhao, Yanrui Du, Haochun Wang, Ming Ma, Wenhao Li, Jingbo Wang, Jiatong Liu, Bing Qin
abstract: Reliable medical reasoning requires LLMs to dynamically access external biomedical evidence to improve factual trustworthiness and reasoning accuracy. However, indiscriminate retrieval can introduce noise and latency, raising a critical retrieval-timing problem: at each reasoning step, the system must decide whether the model's internal knowledge is reliable or external evidence is needed. We propose PUlSE, a lightweight probing method that uses the model's internal representations as intrinsic signals for step-level retrieval control. Our posterior trajectory analysis reveals that erroneous steps exhibit substantially higher inter-layer volatility than correct ones, suggesting unstable internal knowledge. Based on this finding, PUlSE trains a compact probe on inter-layer geometric features to detect factual errors upon step completion, and uses it as an adaptive trigger for retrieval and step regeneration. Across four medical benchmarks, PUlSE-timed retrieval matches exhaustive per-step retrieval in accuracy while reducing retrieval calls by 72%, and can transfer to an unseen legal domain, indicating potential domain-agnostic generality. Overall, our study provides an initial step toward shifting retrieval-trigger design from surface-level confidence estimates to internal activation dynamics for adaptive access.

title: Predicting Unseen Scientific Interactions: Conditional Flow Models Hallucinate Non-Additive Effects
authors: Sam Gijsen, Moritz Seiler, Kerstin Ritter
abstract: Conditional generative models are increasingly used for scientific prediction beyond the direct training support. Yet scientific questions often concern whether one intervention changes the effect of another. Such interactions can be of primary interest while explaining little of the total variation, allowing models to appear accurate overall without recovering the relevant scientific effect. It remains unclear how these models learn interactions and when these successfully extrapolate to unseen conditions. We therefore study interaction recovery in flow-matching models using a physiological time-series simulator, drug dose-response data, combinatorial cell perturbations, and molecular conformer generations, where we separate recovery from hallucinated interaction structure. In the controlled setting, individual effects are learned much earlier than interactions and models hallucinate interactions where none exist. Across settings, we find qualitatively different generalization problems, with successful prediction depending on whether condition structure continues from observed to held-out targets. When it does, interactions are recoverable. If not, models can generate plausible responses while missing the interaction. We furthermore find that hallucinations increase as targets become less identifiable, and that successful interaction recovery in output space can fail under nonlinear readouts. Finally, we show that aggregate fidelity metrics can conceal whether models learn and extrapolate interactions.

title: Neural POS Tagging for the Low-Resource Saraiki
authors: Usman Nawaz, Muhammad Junaid Iqbal, Muhammad Asaf, Mariam Munsif Mir, Faisal Rehman, Tahir Alyas, Muhammad Hasnain
abstract: Part-of-speech tagging is a fundamental sequence labeling task and an important component for many downstream natural language processing applications. However, Saraiki, written from right to left in a Perso-Arabic script, remains an under-resourced Indo-Aryan language, despite being spoken as a mother tongue by 28,849,579 people (approximately 28.9 million) according to Pakistan 7th Population and Housing Census 2023. This paper presents a manually annotated Saraiki Universal POS tagging dataset developed from plain-text. We annotated the text with 17 POS categories. We evaluate three pretrained transformer encoders under the same fine-tuning setup: XLM-RoBERTa base, Urdu RoBERTa small, and multilingual DistilBERT. Experimental results over five random seeds show that XLM-RoBERTa base achieves the best performance, with 87.29% +/- 0.21% development accuracy and 88.60% +/- 0.21% test accuracy. Urdu RoBERTa small and multilingual DistilBERT also provide competitive results, suggesting that multilingual and related-script pretrained encoders are effective for Saraiki UPOS tagging. The dataset, evaluation setup, and baseline results introduced in this work provide a benchmark for future research on Saraiki NLP and low-resource sequence labeling.

title: A new generalization of parking functions: $ρ$-Naples parking functions
authors: Luca Ferrari, Francesco Verciani
abstract: We introduce a new model of parking functions, called $ρ$-Naples parking functions, in which each car has a certain number of spots to check preceding its preferred one before looking for available spots by moving forward. This notion, where each car has its own number of previous spots to check, generalizes that of Naples parking function, where this number is the same for all cars. We start by showing that, for a given sequence of preferences for each car, a successful parking strategy (that is, an assignment of how many backward spots each car is allowed to check) remains successful if we increase the number of backwards spots to check for some of the cars. This means that the set of successful strategies for a given parking preference is an up-set in the lattice of parking strategies, which raises the intriguing question of characterizing such up-sets. Though we are not able to completely solve this problem, we provide a characterization of those successful strategies which minimize the total number of allowed backward steps for a given parking preference, and we determine a lower bound for the number of cars which are allowed to move backwards (also showing that it can be attained). To conclude, we analyze the specific situation in which each car can take at most one backward step, and we completely characterize the set of successful parking preferences in this case.

title: Anuvani-LID: Robust and Calibrated Spoken Language Identification for Indian Languages
authors: Stephen Fernandes, Narayan Choudhary
abstract: Every multilingual speech pipeline begins with a language decision, an error there propagates silently through recognition, translation and routing. In India it spans 22 scheduled languages across four language families, heard over short, noisy, narrowband and code-mixed audio. Foundational speech models increasingly present language identification (LID) as an inherent latent, generalized capability. Autoregressive decoders in speech models emit a special language ID token, and modern LLMs with audio capabilities can name the language when prompted. We test this assumption on identical clips and find that whisper and similar speech models has tokens for only 15 of the 23 languages, on one second inputs Gemini 3.5 Flash reaches 0.52 macro-F1 and GPT-audio 0.14. We present Anuvani LID, a dedicated 115M parameter LID conformer model trained on 54,643 hours of Indian speech spanning 22 Indian languages and Indian accented English. Along with designed and controlled studies on 102 condition benchmark with speaker and corpus held out tests. Across 37 conditions, it reaches 0.914 mean macro-F1, 5.2 points above Gemini 3.5 Flash and ahead of 14 other systems. It is 24 points ahead of Gemini at one second, scores 0.897 on all 23 languages where no other system exceeds 0.713, and is calibrated to an ECE of 0.008. Reliable Indian LID still requires a robust, dedicated and calibrated model.

title: Constrain the Size of Broad Line Region in NGC 1068 Using Sub-millimeter Excess
authors: Qi Guo, Junzhi Wang, Lingrui Lin, Yuqiang Li, Zhi-yu Zhang, Fengyao Zhu
abstract: Constraining the size of broad-line region (BLR) close to the accretion disk in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) is key to understand the central engine and evolution of AGN. We propose a new method to constrain the BLR size, based on millimeter to sub-millimeter spectral energy distribution (SED), from which a sub-millimeter excess may be found. Such excess can be used to determine the solid angle of the free-free emission region from BLR, as a region with high electron density and optically thick at sub-millimeter wavelength for free-free continuum. Millimeter to sub-millimeter SED analysis toward the central source S1 in a nearby type II AGN NGC 1068 was done, which gave an upper limit on the solid angle of BLR region as(4.94 +/- 0.61) *10^-6 arcsec^2, corresponding to a radius no more than 0.085 pc. Such a constraint on the BLR size is important for estimating the masses of central supermassive black holes in AGNs.

title: Contrastive uncertainty learning for robust multi-structure segmentation in lower-pelvic MR
authors: Bilal Sidiqi, Yipei Wang, Wen Yan, Shaheer U. Saeed, Daniel C. Alexander, Yipeng Hu
abstract: Boundary delineation of anatomical structures in prostate MRI is often compromised by regional ambiguity. Automated segmentation methods relying on global overlap loss functions tend to be insensitive to surface deviations, leading to significant errors in ambiguous regions. Most existing uncertainty-aware methods treat uncertainty as a post-hoc quality indicator or prediction filter. We propose Contrastive Uncertainty Learning (CUL), a supervised framework that uses predictive uncertainty to directly guide representation learning. Using Monte Carlo Dropout, CUL identifies voxel-wise uncertainty and structures the embedding geometry accordingly: low-uncertainty, correctly predicted features form stable voxels while high-uncertainty or misclassified features are actively repelled, preventing feature collapse at difficult boundaries. We evaluate CUL on a 589-scan 3D prostate MRI multi-structure segmentation task (8 anatomical structures) using a ViT with UperNet decoder architecture. Average Dice ($83.38\%$) remains comparable to the baseline ($83.35\%$), while surface distance decreases significantly ($p<0.001$) across 6 of 8 anatomical structures. A hard-case analysis reveals a $22{\times}$ asymmetry between significantly improved and degraded cases ($18.8\%$ vs $0.9\%$). Ablation studies show that removing uncertainty-guided sample selection eliminates improvements for the transition zone, while replacing the contrastive objective with a boundary loss additionally removes bladder improvements, demonstrating that both uncertainty-guided sampling and the contrastive objective are essential for the observed gains. These findings demonstrate that the proposed uncertainty-guided representation learning is a useful mechanism for reducing the risk of extreme errors in safety-critical medical segmentation

title: Robust Data-Driven Controller Synthesis from Sampled and Uncertain Frequency Response Estimates using Integral Quadratic Constraints
authors: Luuk Marceau Spin, Maurice W. P. M. H. Heemels, Nathan van de Wouw, Roland Toth
abstract: In this paper, we develop a novel MIMO controller synthesis method that relies solely on frequency-domain data of discrete-time systems. The approach is based on an iterative design procedure using \emph{integral quadratic constraints} (IQCs). It generalizes existing data-driven methods that approximate semi-infinite IQC conditions by enforcing them on a finite set of measured frequency points. Such approximations do not provide guarantees on the continuous frequency axis and may fail to capture inter-frequency behavior. We address this limitation by formulating a convex optimization problem that preserves robustness guarantees over the entire frequency range. In particular, the proposed method explicitly accounts for inter-frequency behavior of both plant and controller, leading to certified robust stability and performance. The effectiveness and computational efficiency of the approach are demonstrated using experimentally obtained frequency response data from industrial-grade semiconductor equipment. The synthesized controller is implemented on the physical setup, and its performance is validated in real-time experiments.

title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
authors: Mohsen Iranmanesh, Sina Moradi Sabet, Sina Marefat, Ali Javidi Ghasr, Maxime Newman Nereyabagabo, Kousha Amouzesh, Jaivir Malhi, Vinci Velasco, Alex Chung, Mohammad A. Tayebi
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it -- a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. A patch that blocks that one piece of evidence can therefore look successful while remaining vulnerable to the same vulnerability with some variation. We present P2Patch, a generative adversarial repair system that treats each patch as a new attack target. Starting from a normalized vulnerability finding, an exploitation agent constructs a reproducing proof of vulnerability (PoV), a patching agent repairs the program, and the exploitation agent then attacks the patched program for a distinct same-vulnerability exploit. Every successful exploit becomes a permanent repair requirement, and the final patch must block all PoVs accumulated during the patching process, with construction-time PoVs kept strictly separate from held-out evaluation oracles. Across 101 C/C++ and Java CVE subjects, this adversarial loop surfaces a distinct confirmed exploit in 41% of runs after the patch has already blocked its original construction-time PoV. Against single-pass repair from the same finding using Claude Code, P2Patch raises held-out fix-closed coverage from 78.1% to 84.7% and beyond-upstream coverage from 42.1% to 62.5%. Under the same held-out oracles, it also certifies more attack paths as blocked than recent state-of-the-art agentic repair systems on overlapping subjects. These results show that adversarial testing and independent security oracles expose repair gaps that one-shot validation misses.

title: PAWA: Panoramic Action-conditioned World Modeling for Multiple Agents
authors: Siqi Yang, Yimu Wang, Ziqi Cai, Chengxuan Zhu, Shuchen Weng, Erwin Wu, Zhaofei Yu, Kaipeng Zhang, Boxin Shi
abstract: A multiplayer world model must predict how the independent actions of several players change a shared environment, including changes outside a player's current field of view. A point-of-view (POV) video captures such changes only after they enter its field of view, whereas panoramic video records the surroundings in every viewing direction and has served as an intermediate representation of the world state in recent world models. Learning this task therefore requires synchronized POV and panoramic videos of interacting players together with their actions, yet no existing dataset provides this combination in Minecraft, an established testbed in which players act independently in a shared, modifiable 3D world. We present PAWA, a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer world modeling. The dataset pairs each player's POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions. Its distributed pipeline decouples CPU gameplay capture from GPU rendering, scales beyond 64 simultaneous players, and re-renders each recorded session under new observation configurations without replaying the gameplay. On this dataset, we develop a dual-tower model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video and couples the two streams through cross-attention that aligns tokens observing the same direction in a shared world frame. We further introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that provides many more player codes than existing rotary codes at the same embedding dimension. Experiments show that PAWA outperforms state-of-the-art multiplayer world models in POV prediction quality while also producing high-fidelity panoramic predictions. The dataset and collection pipeline are open source to support further research on multiplayer world models.

title: Chow groups of symmetric products of projective space
authors: Youming Chen, Wenchuan Hu
abstract: We prove that the integral cycle class map for $\SP^d(\PP^n)$ is split injective, with finite cokernel annihilated by $d!$,and we determine the ranks of Chow groups for $\mathrm{SP}^d(\mathbb{P}^n)$. Compatible integral transfer retractions show that $\CH_q(\SP^d(\PP^n))$ stabilizes for $d\geq q$. An explicit nonalgebraic order two class persists under addition of points, producing a split cokernel summand even in the range $q\leq d$ and in the infinite symmetric product. For the smooth configuration open set, we identify the codimension two cokernel with third unramified cohomology and detect its ramification on a rational resolution. In contrast to addition, even multiplicities annihilate a nonzero Chow class.

title: MAEM: Mitigating Recency Bias via a Replay-Free, Capacity-Controlled Dynamic Mixture of Experts for Class-Incremental Graph Learning
authors: Junlin Chen, Wenhao Wang, Junchao Xu, Qingsong Yao, Fei Xue, Li Sun, Xiao Wang, Ruijie Wang
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel on graph-structured data but suffer catastrophic forgetting when classes arrive sequentially. In class-incremental graph learning, predictions are often dominated by recently learned classes, causing severe recency bias. Dynamic expansion can isolate knowledge across sessions, but many methods assume task-incremental settings and require task identities at test time to select branches or heads---information unavailable in class-incremental learning. Learnable routers offer an alternative, yet continual fine-tuning the router on new data can bias routing toward recent components. We propose MAEM, a replay-free, capacity-controlled dynamic mixture-of-experts framework for class-incremental graph learning. MAEM builds representations with Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and trains a dedicated expert for each new session, then freezes it to protect prior knowledge. For routing without task IDs or a shared trainable router, each expert uses a masked autoencoder (MAE); test nodes are assigned to the expert with the lowest reconstruction error, reducing routing-level recency bias. When the expert pool reaches a fixed capacity, MAEM merges the least-used experts via Git Re-Basin alignment and further distills them into a fused expert using topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions (DeepInversion-style), without storing or revisiting historical graph data. On four class-incremental graph benchmarks, MAEM mitigates recency bias, outperforms strong continual graph learning baselines, and keeps model capacity bounded under strict replay-free learning.

title: Photoacoustic-guided reflection-mode wavefront shaping through dynamic biological tissue
authors: Xuan Liu, Sacha Noimark, Wenfeng Xia, Sebastien Ourselin, Tianrui Zhao
abstract: Strong optical scattering limits the depth at which light can be focused and used for imaging in biological tissue. Photoacoustic (PA)-guided wavefront shaping enables non-invasive light focusing in scattering media, but most existing implementations require optical and acoustic access from opposite sides of the sample and a rigidly aligned free-space optical path, which have confined these demonstrations to thin or static samples. Here, we combine a real-valued intensity transmission matrix (RVITM) algorithm with a photoacoustic guidestar (PA-RVITM) in a reflection-mode configuration. Modulated light is delivered through a flexible multimode fiber passing through the central aperture of a focused ultrasound transducer, enabling optical illumination and acoustic detection from the same side of the sample without a free-space combiner. Fiber integration preserved the wavefront shaping performance, and the reflection-mode PA-RVITM system achieved sub-second wavefront optimization with a ~14-fold PA signal enhancement through a diffuser. In ex vivo chicken breast tissue, the enhancement decreased with tissue thickness, reaching ~3.5 through a 2-mm chicken breast layer, with a speckle decorrelation time of ~450 ms. By performing an independent RVITM optimization at each scan position, our system enabled photoacoustic microscopy of a black nylon wire through the same layer, reducing the imaged line width from ~141 μm to ~102 μm, close to the nominal diameter of ~100 μm. This work advances PA-guided wavefront shaping toward a compact, same-side implementation for future biomedical therapeutic and imaging applications.

title: Physics with Radioactive Ion Beams at the Nuclear Science Laboratory
authors: W. S. Porter, D. W. Bardayan, M. Brodeur, C. Dembski, P. D. O'Malley, F. Rivero, W. W. von Seeger, C. Boomershine, O. Bruce, S. R. Carmichael, S. Coil, A. M. Houff, J. J. Kolata, D. Schroeder, A. A. Valverde, R. Zite
abstract: The University of Notre Dame is home to a rich history of nuclear science efforts, including some of the earliest developments in the production and creation of radioactive ion beams (RIBs). The resulting TwinSol facility stands as the longest continuously-operating RIB facility in the United States, and has enabled a wide range of experimental efforts in nuclear structure, astrophysics and fundamental symmetries through in-flight RIBs one to two nucleons from stability. A recent upgrade to TwinSol via a third solenoid constituted the founding of the TriSol facility, which provides cleaner, better-focused RIBs to downstream experiments. In this paper, we present a summary of RIB science at the Nuclear Science Laboratory (NSL) with both TwinSol and TriSol and discuss recent upgrades and future experimental plans at the facilities.

title: $^{16}$O(p,$γ$)$^{17}$F Reaction and the C and O Isotopic Ratios in Red Giant Branch Stars
authors: D. Robb, P. McGlynn, M. Aliotta, C. Ananna, F. Barile, L. Barbieri, D. Bemmerer, A. Best, R. Biasissi, A. Boeltzig, R. Bonnell, C. Broggini, C. G. Bruno, A. Caciolli, M. Campostrini, F. Casaburo, F. Cavanna, G. F. Ciani, T. Chillery, P. Colombetti, A. Compagnucci, P. Corvisiero, L. Csedreki, T. Davinson, R. Depalo, A. Di Leva, Z. Elekes, F. Ferraro, A. Formicola, Zs. Fülöp, G. Gervino, R. M. Gesuè, G. Gosta, Gy. Gyürky, A. Guglielmetti, C. Gustavino, C. Hebborn, G. Imbriani, M. Junker, M. Lugaro, J. Marsh, E. Masha, R. Menegazzo, D. Mercogliano, V. Paticchio, D. Piatti, P. Prati, D. Rapagnani, V. Rigato, M. Rossi, R. Sariyal, R. S. Sidhu, J. Skowronski, O. Straniero, T. Szücs, S. Turkat, M. Vagnoni, S. Zavatarelli
abstract: The $^{16}$O/$^{17}$O isotopic ratio is a widely used tracer of nucleosynthesis and mixing processes in red giant stars. Its value depends on the rates of the proton-capture reactions responsible for the production and destruction of $^{16}$O and $^{17}$O among which the $^{16}$O(p,$γ$)$^{17}$F reaction plays a central role, as it involves both isotopes. This work reports on a new measurement of the $^{16}$O(p,$γ$)$^{17}$F cross section carried out at the Laboratory for Underground Nuclear Astrophysics (LUNA) over a center-of-mass energy range of 200 - 380 keV, a region previously unexplored by experimental studies. Two complementary techniques were employed: prompt gamma-ray detection and activation. The results obtained with the two techniques are consistent within experimental uncertainties. From the measured cross sections and existing literature data, we evaluate a new thermonuclear reaction rate, which is then used to demonstrate how simultaneous measurements of stellar carbon and oxygen isotopic ratios constrain the initial mass and the extent of the mixing events in red giant branch stars. In particular, we demonstrate how the $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C abundance ratio is primarily sensitive to the temperature T$_{\textrm{max}}$ attained during mixing, whereas the $^{16}$O/$^{17}$O abundance ratio is highly sensitive to the initial stellar mass M$_i$. Therefore, simultaneous measurements of these isotopic ratios can disentangle and place stringent constraints on M$_i$ and T$_{\textrm{max}}$, and the remaining uncertainty is now dominated by stellar abundance measurements rather than nuclear-physics inputs.

title: Exact Cap Response and Aperture Selection for Molecular Communication under Aligned Drift
authors: Yen-Chi Lee, Chun-An Yang, Nan Yang
abstract: Spatial reception under directed molecule transport requires balancing useful molecule capture against intersymbol interference (ISI). To characterize this balance, we study a fully absorbing spherical receiver that counts absorption events only within a prescribed cap. Using the known joint first-hitting law under aligned drift, we derive exact cap impulse, cumulative, and eventual responses. We perform stable cumulative evaluation. We then assess the derived responses through particle simulations and time-step comparisons, and demonstrate that our conditional-timing analysis explains when opposite drifts of equal magnitude can favor the same wider aperture. We also show that for the studied geometry and a symbol duration of $0.15$ s, the aperture that maximizes the signal-to-interference difference (SID) increases from $29.13^\circ$ at zero drift to $61.86^\circ$ at a drift magnitude of $40$ $μ$m/s. These results (i) connect joint arrival-time and location statistics to spatial reception design, (ii) characterize the tradeoff between useful molecule capture and ISI, (iii) support SID-based aperture selection for a given drift and symbol duration, and (iv) quantify the SID loss incurred by retaining the zero-drift optimal aperture for the same symbol duration.

title: Design Space Exploration of Reinforcement Learning Configurations for Post-Legalization Placement
authors: Foteini Oikonomou, Maria Pantazi-Kypraiou, George Goudroumanis, Pavlos Stoikos, Athanasios Tziouvaras, Christos Anagnostopoulos, Georgios Karakonstantis, George Floros
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) have recently been explored for VLSI placement optimization, but their effectiveness for post-legalization placement refinement remains unclear. This paper presents a systematic design space exploration of a GNN-Proximal Policy Optimization (GNN-PPO) framework across three ISPD2015 benchmarks. We evaluate 18 configurations covering reward functions, GNN architectures, action spaces, candidate-set sizes, and training strategies. We analyse the results we obtain to identify pitfalls and to assess the prospects and opportunities of the RL methods for post-legalization placement. On top of that we propose a design classification approach to guide the design decisions of RL models.

title: Scaling Multilingual Safety and Reasoning Evaluation through Reasoning-Guided Translation
authors: Zahraa Al Sahili, Ioannis Patras, Matthew Purver
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across languages, yet their safety and reasoning capabilities remain predominantly evaluated in English. Translating existing benchmarks offers a scalable approach to multilingual evaluation, but preserving task-specific meaning across languages presents significant challenges, particularly for harmful requests, mathematical reasoning, and conversational interactions. We introduce a reasoning-guided translation framework for constructing multilingual evaluations designed to preserve the structure and intended meaning of diverse benchmark tasks. Our approach separates translation strategy selection from large-scale generation, combining reasoning-guided configuration selection with task-aware validation, targeted repair, and independent quality screening. Using this framework, we develop a source-aligned evaluation collection spanning seven safety, conversational, and mathematical reasoning resources across 11 languages. The resulting collection achieves 99.94\% coverage of intended item--language pairs in the two subsets requiring repair. Evaluations of open-source LLMs reveal distinct language-dependent vulnerabilities, including inconsistent refusal behaviour and substantial reasoning degradation in lower-resource languages. These findings highlight the importance of task-sensitive benchmark construction and systematic quality assessment for understanding multilingual model behaviour beyond English.

title: Continual pretraining Prostate MRI ViT Encoder for task alignment
authors: Bilal A. Sidiqi, Yipei Wang, Shaheer U. Saeed, Shiqi Huang, Daniel C. Alexander, Yipeng Hu
abstract: Building foundation models for MRI has emerged as a promising direction for advancing medical image analysis and improving accessibility of task specific models. Existing approaches primarily focus on effective pretraining strategies and evaluating their performance across diverse downstream tasks. While these methods show performance gains, limited attention has been given to understanding task alignment between pretraining and downstream objectives. Unlike language models, where the two stages are naturally aligned, such alignment is less evident in vision based applications. Motivated by this gap, we explore continual pretraining. Specifically, continually pretraining a pretrained ViT encoder using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on a prostate segmentation task to enhance task alignment and downstream performance. We further perform layer-wise representational analysis using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to assess representational shifts and their correlation with task outcomes. Our experiments show improved performance in 3 of 6 downstream tasks and comparable results in the others. Our Feature analysis reveals that, for segmentation tasks, continually pretrained encoder features exhibit greater similarity to those of the finetuned encoder than the original pretrained encoder, correlating with observed performance gains.

title: A Topological\-Geometrical Descriptor (TGD) for Scalable and Interpretable Modeling of Two\-Dimensional Carbon Networks
authors: Rômulo Uriel Liberal de Oliveira, Raphael Matozo Tromer
abstract: We introduce a compact Topological-Geometrical Descriptor (TGD) for planar two-dimensional carbon networks. Atomic coordinates are mapped to a periodic planar graph and represented through ring populations, topological-charge statistics, projected ring geometry, and dual-graph defect adjacency. The resulting modeling vector contains 19 physically interpretable features. We evaluate TGD on 120 published planar carbon allotropes using the DFT relative energy per atom with respect to graphene as the target. Repeated five-fold cross-validation with gradient boosting yields a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0826 +/- 0.0138 eV/atom and R2 = 0.803 +/- 0.074. Under the same validation protocol, TGD gives a mean MAE of 0.0828 eV/atom, compared with 0.0929 eV/atom for a 203-feature Matminer representation. We further analyze 360 vacancy-defected graphene configurations spanning 12 vacancy concentrations from 2 to 24 percent. When entire vacancy concentrations are held out, TGD gives a pooled MAE of 0.269 eV/vacancy and R2 = 0.861, outperforming simple baselines based on vacancy concentration alone or non-hexagonal-ring fraction alone. Sensitivity tests show that the inferred edge sets are stable to moderate changes in the adaptive bond factor. Finally, the mean absolute topological charge is examined as a one-variable empirical surrogate for the allotrope dataset and is treated explicitly as dataset-specific rather than universal. These results show that TGD combines compact prediction with direct structural interpretation while making clear the present restriction to single-layer planar carbon networks.

title: Wearable Data Profiling for NDN-Based Smart Healthcare: Performance Comparison with an IP Baseline
authors: Mohammad R. Shakournia, Nasser Yazdani, Carlos T. Calafate
abstract: Smart healthcare IoT requires low-latency and reliable delivery of patient data, yet IP-based communication remains host-centric and offers limited support for mobility, caching, and request aggregation. This paper evaluates a smartphone-centric Named Data Networking (NDN) approach in which a patient's smartphone aggregates sensor streams and publishes a stable latest profile under a consistent name, enabling effective in-network caching. Using ndnSIM simulations on a realistic medical IoT topology, we compare NDN and IP under identical traffic and link conditions. Results show that per-sample naming provides little benefit, but smartphone aggregation with stable naming allows NDN caching to reduce delay after cache warm-up and achieve significantly higher delivery ratios under congestion compared to IP.

title: HGRP: Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Routability Prediction
authors: Yule Sheng, Yue Yuan, Shan Shen, Daying Sun
abstract: Routability prediction enables rapid evaluation of placement quality without routing, providing effective feedback for routability-driven placement optimization. Recent machine learning methods have achieved efficient routability prediction through data-driven approach. However, their prediction performance highly depends on the capability of input representations to capture essential circuit information. To address the limitations of existing circuit representations in simultaneously preserving logical topology, physical layout and routing resource information, this paper proposes HGRP, a heterogeneous graph neural network for routability prediction. HGRP models the cells, nets, and routing grids as distinct types of nodes and explicitly represents topological connectivity, spatial mapping, and grid adjacency, thereby constructing a heterogeneous graph representation that preserves multi-level circuit semantics. Based on the representation, a heterogeneous message passing mechanism is developed to enable information interaction and feature fusion among distinct types of nodes, effectively learning the complex correlations between circuit structures and routing behaviors. Experimental results on the CircuitNet dataset show that HGRP improves F1-score by 18.69\% relative improvements compared with the state-of-the-art in the congestion prediction task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ShenShan123/HGPR.

title: What Makes a Social Agent's Interactions Effective? Learning from Verifiable Outcomes in Paired Worlds
authors: Caixin Kang, Ke Wang, Yuchuan Wu, Xiaoqiang Wang, Ling Li, Bingxue Qiu, Yongbin Li, Yoichi Sato
abstract: Effective social interaction requires more than fluent responses: agents must reach plans that fit the participants' needs and circumstances.
